title: Cheap, big, not very good
body:
UPDATE NOV 5th

This TV is incapable of handling modern streaming apps. Constant freezing / buffering, and a very slow user interface. I can't in good conscience recommend this thing to anyone.

--ORIGINAL REVIEW--

This is, by all means, a very basic and barebones television. Sure, while it may have the Fire TV operating system powering it, that does not mean that it's an overall good experience.

PROS

- Price. Considering the fact you're getting a 55 inch television for less than $500 is pretty impressive.

- It comes with plenty of apps.

- Volume. It gets loud.

CONS

- Build quality. It feels relatively cheap, and is not all that sturdy. Despite putting the legs on (and screwing them in as far as they would go) the TV itself has a noticeable wobble to it. It's secure and won't fall over, but it feels like it might.

- Picture quality. It's not great. Colours are washed out, and the accuracy is not all too great. Even with manual adjustments, it's just not a good picture. (game mode does have decent response times though, but even that is washed out)

- Sound quality. It's bad. Very bad. Even my older Hisense from a few years ago sounds better than this. The sound lacks depth, and is overly tinny. You can modify it to an extent, but it doesn't help much. Just creates an imbalance.

OVERALL

This is not a good TV. If you're able to get it on sale, and just want something for your kids or a family room that you can easily replace every couple of years, then I suppose this does the job well enough. I mean, I paid $350 during a sale. $350 for a 55 inch 4K TV? Not a horrible price for the size. So long as you consider the TV to be something that's disposable, I suppose there's value here. Like, it's so cheap that I don't care if it breaks (like my last Hisense did).

If you're looking for a cheap and big TV, this is a decent option. If you're looking for a good TV, look elsewhere.

title: 4K ALLM, VRR & 120hz in an inexpensive package
body:
Got the 55 inch Q6 model. I’m coming from a Sony Bravia 49 inch from 2017. Drastic difference in TV quality. I’ve never experienced Dolby Atmos Vision and Audio until I got this Q6, very impressed with the quality

For those that say it’s clunky , name one firestick that isn’t , just happens to be that the TV has one built in as it’s UI.

The most recent software for the TV is Android 11 / firestick OS 8.

As with any fire stick or firestick tv you will be introduced to several updates before you can enjoy the TV the way it’s supposed to work.

Color reproduction is pretty accurate , Brightness , HDR is all on point.

The real gem to this TV is that it can do ALLM, VRR and 120hz , perfect for PlayStation 5. I do see a an extremely noticeable difference when playing Call of Duty and Doom Eternal.

When playing movies that are Dolby Vision / Audio , the setting changes to Dolby Vision Bright.

I reviewed every single review on this TV on Amazon before committing to purchase. I have no regrets , there’s a new Fire TV OS that changes the layout and fixes many issues coming soon. At the 240 dollars I got this tv for on prime week, I’d say I got a bargain.

Build quality, the Q6 housing and stands are made of plastic. The screen is glass!, which is a first for me with a 4K TV. Only caveat is reflection issues with the screen. If the sun is beaming through the window the screen will reflect. My advice is to be careful with the screen area , and if you have to, buy an outdoor cover for the TV to keep it protected from mishaps.

Wi-Fi has no issues with my model, Ethernet works the way it’s supposed to.

The remote is identical to the Fire TV 4K MAX remote, it just has a Hisense branding along with a Fire tv branding.

I’m still confident this TV deserves a 5 star rating. Per my purchase and experience with the Q6 55 inch, it’s light years better than my old Sony Bravia 4k that suffered with the “blue backlight issues”.

I think it’s pretty noble for a TV manufacturer to have a more than affordable 55 inch 4k that has the same extras other 4K TVs have at triple the price.

If you want to speed things up a bit on the TV, use an external SSD usb drive as an expansion of the internal memory and move as many apps as you can into it. Some apps don’t transfer at all. In return you do get faster response but not as good as a current 4k max firestick ( 16GB model ) . I’ve read the new Fire OS update with the new layout should make the fire tv experience much quicker.

Not a single regret on this purchase. I’ve bought a $250 Insignia once that was nightmare fuel, this TV, actually made me forget that purchase at almost the same price. Go for it if you’re a gamer, go for it if you enjoy movies in better quality , Go for it if you want to enjoy current gen tech at a reasonably cheap price.

It’s important to note that 120hz sets the screen resolution to 1440p for the PlayStation 5, most games with low latency features for TVs run at this resolution anyway.

Not bad for a 2025 Hisense!

title: This is a really nice TV

That said, in my case, I was replacing an older TV that had a Fire TV Stick 4K on it. I was expecting the Fire TV interface to be better than that since it's all built in. This TV comes with Wi-Fi 5, which is a bit disappointing since the stick had Wi-Fi 6, and my better sticks have Wi-Fi 6e. You would think the newest TV would have a more updated Wifi version. Not a big deal. Most of my smart TVs I just use the sticks versus the TV interface, so I can switch back to the stick if needed. So far the Wi-Fi 5 is doing just fine. Next, if you are restoring from another Fire TV device backup, don't even try using it for a while. Let it do its thing like update the Fire TV version, and all the apps. It's not easy to know where it is in the process. I don't believe there is a way to see the queue, you just get notices that apps are ready to use. Give it 30-60 minutes depending on how many apps you have installed. I told it to restore from the existing sticks backup, and then tried to go in and use it right away. I received all sorts of errors with logins. The YouTube app I had to uninstall and reinstall to get it to work at all. Fire TV is sort of it's own special torture anyway, but I think if you wait until it downloads and updates everything you will be happier in the long run. Again, don't let this discourage you from buying it. It works great. Fire TV is just a bit special, especially the Hulu and Paramount+ apps which seem very prone to crashing. I still use it on every TV in my house though.

title: Good picture- but no headphone jack and erratic performance. One star for poor software.
body:
Mixed feelings about this monitor... overall disappointed. The picture is crisp. Text is easily readable. I can read text I never could before, and I'm seeing colors I never saw before. The QLED lives up to its rep. So why am I giving it 2 stars? Five reasons:

1) The quality of the software and operation is poor-- as mentioned by other reviewers. My set has a problem of going black every so often and needing to be turned off and back on to regain the picture. This is very obviously a software problem that needs to be fixed.

2) Major: the 43in and 50in versions do NOT contain a headphone jack-- and the advertising didn't state that. They showed the controls from the 55in+ sets. A TV without a headphone jack causes problems if one wants to watch TV while the rest of the family is sleeping or studying... or if a person is hard of hearing and uses headphones all the time... or if one lives in an apartment complex with TV / stereo volume limitations. Its having Bluetooth does not replace a standard headphone jack (I paid for my deluxe, awesome-sound, wired headphones and I want to use them).

3) The color can be difficult to adjust if you're using it as a computer monitor, even if you are using no other input. It seems a regular battle between the Hisense settings and Graphics Card Control panel settings. It should have no problem with this, since it has a specific GAME MODE function built in when hooked into digital feed systems. It took me longer to adjust this than any other TV I've ever owned. In addition, the Game Mode is really annoying, as Hisense seems to find it necessary to visibly inform you every time the TV switches to Game Mode (which is often. It seems to decide to switch to Game Mode at random-- even when it's used permanently as a computer monitor).

4) When used as a computer monitor (which worked just fine on the prior Hisense 43" system) it doesn't always auto-switch to GAME MODE when turning the system on, which significantly affects color and monitor settings. It also often does not recognize the computer as being connected. I contacted Hisense and after them putting me through a dozen hoops, I told them I was returning the television. A few days later I got an email from Toshiba (evidently the manufacturer) which told me exactly how to get my preferred input to start up. It was a setting buried deep, deep inside the system menu... with no manual (either printed or online) to explain to customers where to find such things. So it does boot to the correct HDMI port now, but what I had to go through to find out how to do that was ridiculous.

5) There are several software glitches. Numerous 1-star reviews here point to their internal software as their major complaint. I have to agree. In addition, they present standard advertising on their Home splash screen, and the customer has no way to control that (that I'm aware of). I didn't buy this TV for them to force no-opt-out advertisements on me, taking up a LOT of valuable screen space that could be better used by menu items.

In short, this television is a mess. I would give it 2 stars ONLY because it has a great picture at a low price-- when it works. Since it sometimes doesn't work, 1 star.

This is my second Hisense. I had none of these problems with the prior 43" 4K model. So I'd guess the software team really rushed this one to market... and they need to do some debugging and updating. In addition they seemed set on killing the golden goose by sucking as much profit out of this as possible in forced 3rd-party advertising.

These are major issues... and it cost them stars on this one. Getting this during Prime Days -- and QLED monitor for $199???-- could not resist. But I'm not impressed with system functionality or unwanted ads replacing needed screen space.

ADDENDUM: Today AMAZON support called me, and was super-friendly and supportive. They were very interested in any and all feedback. I also found out a couple of things: 1) This is an Amazon Fire TV. For some reason something didn't click with the "SMART FIRE" labeling on the advertisement, and I didn't realize this was an Amazon television. So if you like Amazon products, this has the stuff. If not, that's something to be aware of. 2) Apparently there IS online documentation on this television... but it is buried deep in the HELP area of the Amazon website, and can be tricky to find. It's not a typical technical manual; written more for the end user... which is good (unless you're looking for technical information).

I mentioned to Amazon I would put a big bright orange card in the box telling people how to find help setting up the TV. They accepted all my feedback, and couldn't have been more supportive and friendly. I have always found Amazon support to be top-notch... which I can't say for the Hisense team.

So overall, now that I know exactly how to set up and use the TV... it works most of the time. I still don't like that it doesn't have a headphone jack, nor that 1/2 of the Home screen is taken up in 3rd-party advertising rather than menu functions, or that every once in a while it decides to go dark. But one thing I've experienced with Amazon is that they are VERY concerned with customer welfare and feedback (in most instances). They want Amazon products to be quality and popular, and their support system shows it. Of course I would have appreciated it if that support had been available a couple of weeks ago, but on the plus side within that two weeks I was contacted by both Toshiba and Amazon, both concerned with my satisfaction regarding this product.

It still remains that they need to correct the software / performance / advertising issues on this television. I didn't buy this system to have advertising thrown in my face every time I turn it on, and I sure expect it to work instead of dropping to black. I give it one star for erratic performance, poor software, and forced advertising on the home screen.

title: One of the easiest TVs to setup to get great picture quality
body:
I got this TV for our guest bedroom because it provides the latest in video formats while providing excellent picture quality. The QD6 series from Hisense is part of their Hi-QLED range. I have always appreciated the beautiful, vivid colors of Hisense QLED TVs, and this one is no exception. It provides 4K Ultra HD resolution and upscaling, native 60Hz with 120 motion rate processing, Dolby Vision and HDR10+ support and more. I have the TV sitting on top of a bedroom dresser, so its very thin profile and small stand fit perfectly while ensuring stability. This TV is very light at just 12.2 kg. I got the 50" version as it is the perfect size for our guest room.

One of my favorite aspects of this TV is that it runs on Fire OS. I have Fire TV sticks for my other TVs, so setting this one up was simply a matter of logging in with my Amazon account. It automatically configures WiFi and even downloads the same apps that I have on my other Fire TV devices. The TV got a couple of firmware updates as well as the remote control when I first set it up. It was seamless and only took a few minutes. The remote is basically a Fire TV stick remote with some extra buttons for settings and inputs. The one thing that really stood out on this TV, even compared to other Hisense TVs, was how quick I was able to dial in a great picture. Selecting Filmmaker mode looked great, and I simply enabled Dynamic Contrast and Dynamic Color to High, set sharpness to the center value (50), and disabled any of the motion processing. Immediately I found the color temperature to be perfect (not too warm, and not too cool), the skin tones were natural, the brightness was punchy without blooming and the colors were vivid without blooming either. The contrast was very good, giving the picture a natural look where blacks were dark without crush or much grey. I did have to configure each input type manually as not all types (like SDR compared to HDR10) have the same picture settings available. There are more advanced settings to really dial in the screen but I really did not have to tweak anything at that level. The menus are responsive and very simple to use, especially if you are already familiar with Fire OS. I find the interface is similar to other TV operating systems so it is quick to navigate to your favorite streaming app from the menu, or just press the button on the remote for the dedicated apps. Normally I will always recommend a sound bar or full home theater setup, but the speakers on this TV are fine for basic, everyday use. Voices are clear but there is not much bass. There are 3 HDMI inputs (all support 4K 60Hz), a digital optical out, two USB ports, an antenna input and even an Ethernet port. This TV also has a Game Mode to reduce input lag, but keep in mind that it only supports up to 60Hz.

For our use as a guest room TV, this Hisense QD6 is an excellent addition to the room. I really appreciated how fast and simple it was to configure a great looking picture while Fire OS allowed me to instantly set up this TV to match my other Fire OS devices. Very highly recommend it!

title: Very good TV, worth the cost for upgrading from older TV
body:

Pros:

- The image is incredible. My previous TV was 4K, but this one with the mini leds and Dolby Vision is amazing. Even for contents that are in a format inferior to this, I still find it great. The image seems so much more realistic

- The size is perfect for my living room, which is not super big, but not tiny either (I am on a 1-bedroom apartment)

- TV settings for changing the brightness of the image is very easy to access while you watch tv (there is a shortcut), making it easy to change during the day

- My place is very bright with sunlight, and the image and blacks seem very good

- I really like that the remote is backlit, so you can see the buttons in the dark when you hold it.

- Installation was very easy, and I did it alone (30's female)

Cons:

- The anti-reflective surface is less than I imagined it would be. It's not super bad, but it doesn't completely not reflect either. I am in a very bright room, so this was super important to me.

- The sound seems normal for a TV, is stereo I would say. I didn't have much opportunity to test this as I use a soundbar, but I like the sound more focused and directed at me.

Others:

- I can't comment on the smart TV features as I use Apple TV, so I only used the original OS when setting it up. It was not smooth, but it was fine.

- I mainly use for TV and YouTube, I don't play video games on it, so I can't say if it is good for that or not.

Overall I would recommend this TV if you are upgrading from an older model, you will see the difference! I would say it is worth what it costs.

title: Feeble sound limitation Bluetooth headphones. Heavily locked down GoogleTV Android version.
body: I bought the Hisense 75U78QG expecting a good mid-range TV, but the software experience has been really disappointing. The picture quality is good for the price, but the Google TV firmware on this model is one of the most restricted versions I’ve ever seen. Here are the main problems: 1. Bluetooth audio is extremely low Connecting AirPods or any Bluetooth headphones results in very quiet audio. There are no Bluetooth audio controls, no Absolute Volume toggle, no headphone mode, no sound format options, nothing. You’re stuck with whatever the TV decides, and it’s barely usable for wireless listening. 2. You cannot install any APK or third-party apps This model comes with a “Fully Managed Mode” firmware (FFM), which means: • “Install Unknown Apps” is completely removed • Cannot sideload any apps. • USB and Downloader apps are blocked 3. Very limited sound settings For some reason, Hisense disabled half of the normal Google TV sound menus. There’s no Dolby toggle, no PCM option (unless HDMI/optical is active), no advanced tuning, and no Bluetooth gain settings. For a “Devialet Company tuned” TV, the audio control is ironically the most restricted part. 4. Software feels unfinished Even basic Android TV settings are missing. It feels like Hisense shipped a half-locked corporate firmware instead of a full consumer OS. Google TV 14 should be powerful, but this build is heavily stripped down. The bottom line: If you only need a big screen for streaming from the Play Store and nothing else, the TV is fine. But if you expect: • Normal Bluetooth volume • Ability to install APKs • Side load Android Apps • Full Google TV settings • Better audio configuration This model will frustrate you. I wish I knew this before buying. Hisense should clearly mention that this TV uses a restricted Android TV build.

title: Great TV Overall, Wish AirPlay Worked However
body: Got this TV and have been testing it out for about 3 weeks now. The TV itself is very easy to set up, basic plug and play. It was many ports including HDMI eARC for audio (great if you want to hook up a sound bar). I also note the high refresh rate ports which make gaming amazing on this. Besides from the generic set up, the TV uses android TV which means that you can download any apps you want making this a super customizable option relative to other TV operating systems out there. The software set up was very easy and took 5 minutes after the firmware update. Everything can be done via your phone by scanning the QR codes on the TV I tested the picture quality on the TV in all resolutions up to 4K and it looked stunning in all aspects. The colors are great (not OLED level, but very close) and the upscaling of lower resolutions is fairly noticeable (in a good way, it makes it look better). The audio quality is also very great as the TV has many speakers and bass on the back which adds to the surround sound. I currently have this sitting in our bed room and it makes movies and tv shows a pleasure to watch, especially with the high refresh rate. Now on to the only bad encounter I have had with this TV... The airplay does not work properly when connecting via my laptop. The screen simply goes black and the TV freezes, eventually crashing out of airplay. This is a major bummer for me as I love to play things on my laptop and airplay it to the TV. Airplay works fine when using it with a phone which is super weird. I looked up this issue online and found that others also have had this exact same issue for months with this brand and it has yet to be fixed. This is a large downside for me personally. The workaround is to obviously just hook up the laptop via HDMI, but this can be a hassle and is not convenient. In my 3 weeks of testing this TV, this is the only downside I have encountered. The other aspects of this TV (picture quality, high refresh rate, sound quality, and ease of use) make this TV an easy recommendation. However, if you need airplay to work properly, this may not be for you

title: Old tv was from 2016, this a massive upgrade
body:
Had an LG from 2016, which was discontinued in 2017 (dang it). Didn't realize I was using broken software for almost 10 years (hdr settings were always choppy). Needless to say the upgrade to this 65" Hisense is an eye opener (literally, lol). Physically it looks better than my previous (no large grey plastic edges) and has better port locations (previous tvs ports location caused cables to bend at 90 degrees, broken a few). The software interface actually looks great (previous tv couldn't launch smart features anymore) and apps are easy to install. Easily connected to my Google account and integrated all my account settings without issues (YouTube settings, disney plus profiles, etc). I have it connected to a Lenovo Legion desktop running a RTX 5070 with 64gb of ram. First game I played on the Hisense tv was Stellar Blade. Was able to run at 165hz with no issues, looked ridiculous (details everywhere, background was clear, Eve's ponytail flowed like water, and I was able to actually block, thought I was just old, lol). I next tried Battlefield 6 and this is when smart features took over and picture automatically switched to HDR10+ (awesome no need to constantly look to the best options). Again game looked ridiculous, my accuracy went when wwwaaayyy up. I then watched a few older CGI movies to see how the tv would handle them (Starship Troppers Invasion 1080p, Appleseed 1080p, and Final Fantasy VII Advent Children 2160p 4K). Didn't notice much difference with Staship, the Hisense did a great job cleaning up the picture. Appleseed is where I started to see what the Hisense 65" Hi-QLED could do. The tv thought movie was a game and ran it with game settings. All the colors absolutely popped, the Ai features added details to skin and metal. Then Advent Children is where I noticed a huge difference. All the clothing in the movie had added texture and lighting, skin absorbed light properly (no shiny foreheads, lol), and details were highlighted in a way that made the experience seem like a different movie (context, watched Advent Children everyday for a year leading up to the release of FFVII Remake). The settings interface is a little clunky and some options seem like there in the wrong category, but that's a personal choice. Sound options are great, both Atmos and DTX, switches automatically depending on what is being viewed. Connected to 5.1 home theater through ARC and tv now controls home theater (volume up and down, but no other options available) with no sound lag to be heard. Light up buttons on tv remote is a handy feature. I highly recommend this tv, especially if it's on sale, especially if you're looking to upgrade from a 10 year old tv.

title: Great TV, bad customer service
body: I purchased the 75-inch Hisense U7SG during the Prime Day deal for $999. Unfortunately, after unboxing the brand-new TV, I discovered multiple dead/stuck pixels on the panel. I contacted both Amazon and Hisense, but neither has been willing to offer a replacement. Amazon’s only option is to return the TV for a refund, which puts me in a difficult position because the same TV is now selling for around $1,999. Hisense also opened a support case, and I even escalated it to Tier 2 support, but so far they do not seem to consider the visible pixel defects significant enough to justify a replacement. As a Lead Quality Engineer myself (although in the software field), I find this extremely disappointing. A brand-new premium TV should not arrive with visible panel defects, and I would expect the manufacturer to stand behind the quality of its product (especially when the issue was present right out of the box). What makes this even more frustrating is that I actually think the U7SG is an excellent TV. The picture quality, features, and especially the gaming capabilities are impressive. I was seriously considering Hisense for future TV purchases as well. Unfortunately, this experience with their quality assurance and customer support has completely changed my opinion. For comparison, I previously had a similar panel issue with an LG C5 OLED purchased from Best Buy. The TV was replaced immediately with a brand-new unit, and the replacement had no panel issues. I understand that manufacturers may have pixel policies and tolerances, but visible dead/stuck pixels on a brand-new TV should still be considered a defect. If this is now considered “acceptable” panel quality, that’s very disappointing. A great TV is only as good as the company standing behind it when something goes wrong.

title: The new version is worth the money and a significant upgrade 10 out of 10
body:
Hisense 65U88QG - 65" 4K Smart Mini-LED PRO Google TV (2025 Model)

So this is my first TV upgrade in over 15 years so I spent an insane amount of time researching the best TV I could get for my money and can I say I went down one of the largest rabbit holes for about a week and a half learn stuff that the average TV viewer probably doesn't need to know and I landed with this TV after all that research.

So I decided to get the 65 over the 55 honestly with my setup 55 would have been perfect the 65 is insanely huge for retrospect I've never had a TV that's this big in my life I normally stick to like 40 and 32. Let me tell you the things I learned about:

- the brightness is different on every size TV even if it's advertised as 5000...

- the display type is also different per TV size some being ADS & VA.

- the sound quality improves based on the size of the TV.

At first I thought wow that's a lot of brightness maybe it's too much well... didn't really need to ask that question because I can turn the brightness down the TV not to mention the 65-in only hits about 3,000 ish. Now the reason I went for the 65 inch over the 55 was due to the fact that the display type was VA which has many more advantages over an ADS display type, the dimming zones are also higher with the 65 at 2048 meaning it already has double that of the 55 inch which means better picture quality.

Now if you're curious about the difference in ads versus VA panels here you go:

VA: slower response times. Superior contrast and brightness which enhances HDR, deeper blacks, higher brightness.

ADS: in short it has reduced of everything above although it offers higher response times which can reduce blur but it's super minor. It's also less ideal for a dark room but it has much wider viewer angles making it better for off-centered seating.

Now personally I'm a heavy gamer but I'm also a super big movie buff so a VA was the best option for me. My overall experience has been amazing it arrived in one day and it wasn't damaged, I definitely don't need a soundbar it's incredibly loud the subwoofer is insane and it can also be turned off if it's too much maybe if you have a bigger area then it might be worth it but I would say hold off and make the decision after you get the tv. the picture quality is immaculate it blows my mind away I would say it's incredibly close to OLED picture quality (this information has been quoted from many sources and tons of research) it is even better since mini LEDs are completely immune to burn in with the amount of time I will be spending on this TV that's incredibly important. I've tested the HDR capabilities the IMAX and the GAMING all have completely blown me away I'm incredibly excited to start doing home premieres as where I live the quality of this TV is definitely better than what's offered in the theaters anyone who says it has bad color need them eyes checked asap. Set up took a little bit of time would definitely be harder with a single person. Overall 10 to 10 TV in my opinion I would definitely say to go for the 65 over the 55 if you're having a really hard time deciding I hope that this review helped you. Side note I definitely would have posted pictures but my setup is not complete yet.

title: Hisense 55U88N an excellent replacement for Amazon Fire TV ML55F700
body:
Wow! This is a significant upgrade from the Amazon Fire TV 55" Omni Mini-LED Series, QLED 4K UHD smart TV (Model ML55F700) I bought in November 2024. I decided to purchase this TV because the ML55F700 does not work with my Logitech Harmony Home Hub (I tried everything imaginable and had an open tech support case with Logitech for several months). Logitech recently posted information revealing that Amazon intentionally closed their remote API controls and ecosystem to prevent third party product development.

The Hisense 55U88QG worked instantly with the Harmony Home Hub system, although I did have to tell the Harmony system that I was using a 55U8N television because the 55U88QG wasn't available in the list of models. I did this following the advice from Microsoft CoPilot. Harmony Home Hub accepted it and I have all the control functionality I was expecting.

This Hisense (55U88QG) TV is similar in cost to the Amazon Fire TV but the specs are significantly better. The brightness of the screen is remarkable (up to 5000 nits) and the black content in images really does look black. It works with my Harmony Home Hub system seamlessly. I've only had the television for one day but so far it's performed leaps and bounds better than my Amazon ML55F700.

I use a Sony home theatre system for sound so I can't fairly compare the sound of the Hisense TV to that. The Hisense does have better sound than the Amazon Fire TV, which is to be expected because it's comparing (Amazon ML55F700) 2.1 Dolby Atmos sound to (Hisense 55U88QG) multi-channel 4.1.2 sound.

The Hisense TV is thicker than the Amazon Fire TV. I expect this is to support the two subwoofers that are built into it as well as making space for the sound to travel out the top and sides of the television.

I've been watching the 2026 Winter Olympics. The upscaling to 4K is remarkable, with the detail and colors far more detailed compared to the Amazon ML55F700. When I switch to a true 4K source, the image is breathtaking; it's like looking through a window.

The Hisense TV does have Google TV and all the apps I normally would use are available there; setup was simple. No regrets: I'm not missing using the (slower) Amazon Fire TV interface. During setup you'll have the option to limit what Google collects for information; my IT background strongly urges you to restrict information collection.

I know it's only been a day using it but so far this Hisense television has exceeded my expectations. I recommend it.

Unfortunately, on December 29, I noticed a solid black line running horizontally across the screen, about three inches from the bottom. This happened after only five days of normal use.

I contacted Amazon first, but they told me to reach out to the manufacturer. Hisense initially responded quickly, so I was hopeful. After that, communication stalled. I sent a follow‑up email, and they replied saying they understood my frustration and would get back to me within 24 hours. When that didn’t happen, I sent a third email requesting an update and received no response at all.

I then tried to return the TV through Amazon, only to be told I would have to pay for shipping and be responsible for packing the unit myself, despite it being defective almost immediately after arrival.

For a premium TV with such impressive specs, I expected far better support from both Amazon and Hisense. The product performed beautifully at first, but the sudden failure and lack of meaningful customer service have been incredibly disappointing. I’m now stuck with a nearly brand‑new TV ($1000) that already has a major defect and no clear path to resolution.

I will provide an update should an improved service become available.

title: very good mid-range TV with some highlights and quirks
body: We've had the chance to use TVs from a variety of manufacturers over the last few years, ranging from Sony to Samsung to LG and now this, our first Hisense. I'll try to keep this brief and would suggest you go see one of these in person before committing. Highlights: • GREAT operating system! Hands down, you should try to get a TV with the GoogleTV OS - it's the least bloated, fastest, easiest to use option • excellent colours, brightness, clarity - images and motion pop, making it a treat for action films, video games, whatever • very good sound - with a lot of modern, "flat" TVs, there's not a lot of room for speakers, resulting in tinny, narrow sound. Hisense has managed to put a reasonable number and size of speaker drivers in the body of the base behind the screen and they don't make odd rattling noises either when driven to a reasonable level Quirks: • somewhat limited "off-axis" viewing, though not awful - if you're trying to gather a dozen buddies on multiple couches across a rec-room, some are gonna be fighting for the centre spot. For modest sized crowds though, they'll get a fine viewing experience • highlights next to shadows tend to show some bleed across ("blooming") particularly if you're viewing in a dark room There are not a lot of TVs in this price-class with GoogleTV OS and such good sound without a soundbar. If you have a chance to try several side by side, do it - I think you'll find you'd generally have a spend a lot more to upgrade all aspects of this TV. As such, it's a good value as it's priced right now, right around the thousand dollar mark. Docked a star for the quirks but it still gets a recommend.

title: Bright, Feature-Rich TV with Minor Drawbacks
body: The Hisense 55U88QG (2025 Model) is an impressive 4K Smart Mini-LED PRO TV that punches well above its weight. The picture quality is stunning—colors are vibrant, brightness is exceptional even in daylight, and the Mini-LED backlighting adds real depth to HDR content. Gaming is a standout feature here too, thanks to the 165Hz refresh rate and VRR support. The built-in 4.1.2 Dolby Atmos speaker system is surprisingly good for a TV and eliminates the need for an external soundbar in smaller spaces. Google TV runs smoothly, and navigating apps or switching inputs is a breeze. That said, a couple of small drawbacks keep it from being a perfect 5-star product. The viewing angles are a bit limited, and the intense brightness can cause some haloing or blooming in darker scenes. It also has only three HDMI 2.1 ports, which may be a limitation if you have several high-end devices. Still, for the price and feature set, this TV is a fantastic choice—especially for gamers and movie lovers who want premium visuals without a premium price tag.

title: Another solid mid-high tier Hisense tv
body:
So I am a very big movie fan as well as of Tv's. I'm not some sort of professional expert but I would say I am fairly knowledgeable about Tv's compared to most people. So I will try and give as good in depth review as I can. THe setup was extremely easy and everything came in the standard foam protection with cardboard on the front screen. The base install was annoying sort of. It is a two person job and you are supposed to rest the sides on boxes and install it. I found it was just easier to very carefully put it face down on my couch with the bottom hanging off, and screw it in.

The OS itself is using Google TV. Which Hisense in my experience either uses or else Firetv. I do prefer google it seems a bit more snappy and was a super easy setup. Like most OS's it has a decent amount of clutter of ads and stuff you do not want to see, but that is pretty much the norm at this point. It was super easy to setup logging into my google account and everything was seamless. The settings menu is also feature rich with lots of customization. What I like is that when you are watching something you can bring up the audio and video menu, and do changes mid watch so you actually see the difference, surprisingly others do not. You can even get into the more "advanced" setting like brightness and contrast and change it while watching. Rather than bringing up the entire video settings men, switching and then going back to see if

The audio was semi lack luster in terms of range but that has been my experience on literally every television I have owned. It did get super super loud, even at 19 out of 100 it was easy to hear. It has an impressive looking rear speaker as well as ones built in the sides. It looks like it would have deep bass and rich sound. But honestly it is sort of flat. I've tried out multiple brand and ranges from low to mid to high tier flagships. And no matter what you always get a separate sound bar if you are like a serious movie/show watcher especially action stuff where you want a big rich sound. But if this is just for scrolling your favourite comfort sitcom the audio is fine.

The screen quality is pretty good. It uses mini LED's which means it has small LED'S it uses to brighten up certain parts of the screen. This is useful to try and maintain dark or black scenes that have bright spots. Without it you would get whats called "blooming" or "haloing". As you can see from the photo with the black background normally there would be a bunch of white blooming behind the back. The photo shows some but that was my camera to my eye I saw literally zero.without the mini LED's the entire screen would be grey but never black no matter how dark the scene. it also does have the high refresh rate, which worked well with my Xbox gaming. It comes with a "pc/game mode" which basically helps with latency. It was a small difference, the standard modes actually had pretty good latency already. Meaning how long it takes for you to press a button for it to happen on screen. If it has bad latency it will feel sluggish and slow.

It claims it has "obsidian panel". What is that? Well it is marketing. Every company for these mid-higher tier applies their own sort of coating/ film to deal with reflection and light in some ways. Honestly with a direct bright light it doesn't handle it well. But the TV gets so bright it can overcompensate that.

Partly due to the mini LED's but also the screen and processing itself the colours are indeed very bright and vibrant. They don't look overdone or saturated. Just a nice vibrant pop. You can see from the video i took that the brightness levels are amazing. And that is in standard mode not even vivid.I have other OLED televisions as my main TV's and while they are getting better they can't really compete with this. Normally I have to crank brightness to maximum but I find even standard mode is incredibly bright and I often use the darker modes.

The remote itself has all the features you would want. It auto lights up when you pick it up. And while I wish the buttons lights were way brighter it does at least work in a dark room. It also has all the basic buttons you would want without it being cluttered. As well as the "big four" streamers as quick buttons on top which is very nice. I almost exclusively use Youtube so it is good to have that button there because my other tv doesn't.

Now the issue is with pricing. This is Hisense's mid-high tier television. just below the UR9, another television I tested that was very very similar if only a very small step up. But when you compare it to other brands mid-high tier televisions especially the OLED's. Its not that this is a bad television. Its just that while they may have some drawbacks in terms of brightness, in many ways they are superior. And you can get them for either less or a very similar price point. Hisense certainly has made some big strides making more mid-high tier televisions. But just isn't as established as the "big three" other brands. And the television just does not justify being that high when you can get the others as I said.

Still Overall I do recommend it. it did not seem fair to deduct an entire point simply due to the price which can fluctuate and change. It is still a really good and capable television. The image quality, colours and brightness are really good. Google TV is snappy and works as fast as you would expect on a higher end model. The mini LED's handles the black scene, blooming and colours extremely well. Playing my system on it was a very good experience. And the easily customization settings in real time is a feature you surprisingly do not get on all brands TV's. Its better than even my OLED in some ways like brightness, vibrancy, Googletvs snappiness, but certainly not all.

author: Christopher V

title: Impressive!
body:
I have quite a few TV’s around the house including OLED’s, UST projectors, and mini LED’s as well. Since two of my LED’s are this years’ models, I will be referencing those during this review. I will definitely compare the black levels of this Hisense to the OLED quality, but I will mainly focus on the newer mini LED’s.

The lineup:

Samsung M70H 65” On sale for $700 right now (https://www.amazon.ca/dp/B0GSC9VN3Y)

Hisense 75U7SF 75” $2000 (https://www.amazon.ca/dp/B0GJ1958F8)

Hisense UR8 55” $1500 (this one)

Black Levels

While these may not be OLED’s, they all do a pretty good job with black levels. Of course they can’t produce the same deep blacks as an OLED, but it is surprising at how far mini LED’s have come. As expected the less expensive M70 is the worst performing of the bunch, but it still does an excellent job for the price. It suffers from some light bleed on the bottom/top, but overall, if you are looking for a decent TV and don’t need top performance, this is a good choice. The U7 and the UR8 are pretty close, but I do have to give the edge to the UR8. The U7 has just a bit of light bleed on the bottom black bar, but only on the most demanding scenes. In fact, through all my testing I really only noticed it when I was a bit off angle and during specific scenes. One example would be Furiosa from the 17:26-24:45 mark, where it has a high red saturation and I noticed it a bit on the bottom. The UR8 on the other hand did not have this issue when I played the exact same scene. The M70 struggles with most scenes, but it still does a decent job and it is not that noticeable unless, like me, you are really looking for it. All handled shadow detail well, but both Hisense were noticeably better than the Samsung. For reference, I found The Dark Knight and The Batman looked great on all three, but the M70 was the weakest while the two Hisense were pretty much a tie.

Colour/Brightness/Refresh

All three did an excellent job with colour with the M70 coming in last, but not by too much. However, I have to say when I first tried The Watchmen on the UR8, I was pleasantly surprised at how much the colours actually popped compared to the U7. Again this movie looked pretty great on all three, but I am definitely giving the edge to the UR8 for colour reproduction. Brightness was definitely a non issue on each, but the UR8 with 5000 nits was the brightest. Finally, the refresh rates are higher on the more expensive models with the UR8 at 180Hz, U7 at 165Hz, and the Samsung at only 60Hz. While watching sports, I did find the Hisense TV’s did a better job, but the M70 was fine and the slower refresh rate didn’t really bother me all that much. Sorry, but I didn’t do any game testing on any of them.

Sound

I use a 7.2 system for my dedicated home theatre and sound bars for everything else, but I have to say, these companies have done wonders with integrated sound. Again the Samsung is the weakest here and both the U7/UR8 do an excellent job. In fact, they do such a good job, I would daresay you can probably get by without purchasing a sound bar.

Remotes/Stands/Reflection

While the Samsung remote is compact, I prefer both remotes (which are identical) on the Hisense models. All do a great job, but I like the full size version that comes with the Hisense TV’s. I also like the pedestal stands on both Hisense models better since you have more placement options. While they are a bit more difficult to put on, they are heavy “dutier” than the Samsung which has the wide leg design. Both the M70 and UR8 are more reflective than the U7 since it has a matte screen. Even though the UR8 says it has an anti-reflective screen, I found it reflected more light than my U7. Again, the Samsung was the most reflective and even though it is an often discussed topic (dislike of the matte screen), I found the U7 did a great job and there was little degradation in picture quality. This really comes down to personal preference and TV placement (living room vs. dedicated home theatre), so do some research if you are unsure.

Overall, the UR8 is a fantastic television. The colours really pop with the RGB mini LED’s and it does a fantastic job with black levels/shadow details. However, for $500 less (75”), the U7 is a strong contender. On the other hand, if you are looking to save some money and don’t need the deep blacks or high refresh rates, the M70 at $1100 (75”) is a great TV. Just don’t expect it to look as good as the other two. Hopefully I have touched on everything and made your choice a bit easier, depending on your needs. No matter which one you go for, I think you’ll be happy if that’s any help.

Recommended

Good luck with your decision/purchase

title: OLED Quality Without OLED Headaches
body:
I was very excited to test this tv for one reason and one reason only. Will rgb mini led be the end of oleds. And personally I think so.

I tried my best to get the best quality video to show this tv up against an oled monitor but with the sheer amount of brightness it produces it was very hard to get a nice and clean video of the picture. But wow. Is it ever close.

The first thing I will say is if you’re here because you’re on the fence between an oled and a rgd mini led I would personally say get a rgb mini led. As you can see in my video alone the glare difference between the two, the Hisense not even phased, and the worse part is, it’s beside 2 windows and the door. My oled is all the way back of my room only dealing with one window and part of the door.

The obsidian is amazing technology. I can have all my windows blinds open and not lose an ounce of visuals or colour quality whatsoever.

To go further into the picture quality the dimming zones are a whole other experience. The best way I can describe it to anyone is imagine watching a movie, and everyone’s walking through a forest, and a pov angle happens when you look up in the trees. It’s a sunny day so you see very bright spots through the break of trees. Well that’s what happens when you watch that part of the movie, those breaks where the sun are will get very bright, to the point where you’d think you’re looking at the sun. And it does the same if you’re watching something dim, it’ll look dark, but! Not to where you’re squinting to see it. No no. Just dimmed, dark, details there but faded from the lack of light. It is a completely different viewing experience.

Now performance as a rgb mini led, I ran all the testing I could find a lot of it provided by Dolby and it passed everything. No halos, no light bleeding, nothing. It performed great and that was the biggest relief. Was seeing that this was a quality rgb mini led.

For the google tv portion, ya a bit limited but very quick and very fast I will say. Jumping through the apps felt like I was on my personal computer. It was snappy, flawless, and loaded up quickly.

180hz refresh rate made this tv really be a powerhouse for gaming. Running any system and my computer at its max. If actually made couch computing a thing in my house hold again. As prior too I didn’t want to not play on the oled, now it’s hey why not. Now I will say the response time is not an oled instant response time. I did look up and down and could not find an advertised response time anywhere but if I had to guess from my experience we’re sitting in the 2-4ms range.

Audio wise the sound system built in packs a punch. I would definitely tell you no sound system is needed. You can have a very movie theatre like experience from this TVs integrated system alone. It had great mids, a very impressive low bass, and good eqs. The Dolby sound came with the ability for dialogue enhancements as well which I found to be great.

I actually have this tv pair up with Hisense AX5140Q and together they really hit with quality. I ran the tv in HI Connect and found that it really dialed in the eqs. Everything seemed very on point, there was no dramatic volume increases, and it just provided a good rich sound quality.

With everything being said, it sounds complicated and it can be going through all the settings, but luckily I will say Hisense has the presets pretty locked in to where you can get the picture quality shown just off of them. There is also build in AI colour control what I have been playing with and can’t find any major flaws. It’s basically changing the colour profile based on what is happening/you’re doing.

Game mode was an instant kick over once setting up my system, and put everything to give the best performance while allowing me to swap HDRS to game hdr but also jumping through its own presets for “type of game” almost like a monitor.

With all that being said. I can recommend it.

It’s the best of all worlds in my opinion. It’s not a fragile oled that you look at and it gets a scratch.

You don’t have to have the perfect room and lighting for it to perform it just performs. And I found it had the best of both worlds, if you want some insane rich crazy colour palate you can get it, but then if you want accuracy and everything to look as pure as it’s suppose to look you have imax mode a click of a button away giving that to you.

Very impressive tv, and very impressive technology. I’m looking forward to see how far this goes because we’re off to a strong start and a very high bar set.

My only gripe with this TV is how bright it is even when turned all the way down and every setting tweaked. I am otherwise a huge fan of this TV. title: THICK BOY
body:
🌟 Quality:

The build quality on this TV is absolutely excellent. It features a premium, solid, and very heavy included stand that provides total peace of mind when it comes to stability. The remote control is equally well built, feels solid in the hand, and includes a great backlit feature so you can see almost all the buttons in the dark. It even comes with remote batteries included. One thing to note is that the TV is actually quite thick, which is likely due to the massive built-in sound system. While the initial setup was relatively straightforward, the physical assembly instructions could have been a little clearer, and a QR code linking to a live video setup would have been helpful.

⚙️ Functionality:

The picture quality on this 4K RGB Mini-LED display is truly something else—it is easily the best Mini-LED screen I have ever seen, producing exceptionally deep blacks. However, while the Obsidian Panel anti-reflection coating works fine when content is playing, the screen remains quite reflective on a fully black desktop background, especially if you look at it from a side angle.

The audio performance is superb and gets incredibly loud—loud enough to host a house party—thanks to the built-in 4.1.2 channel Dolby Atmos system and subwoofer. You can genuinely feel the bass during sports and movies, though it is not quite as punchy as a dedicated external sound system.

On the technical side, this TV overdelivers. While the 180Hz refresh rate is officially designated for HDMI 1 and HDMI 2 (after toggling the HDMI format to "Enhanced Pro" in the settings), I was able to successfully achieve 4K at 180Hz with HDR enabled using the USB-C input on my laptop. Dropping the resolution down to 1440p allowed the refresh rate to crank all the way up to 330Hz, verified via Test UFO. It also features AMD FreeSync Premium Pro, and it worked perfectly with G-Sync on my graphics card once enabled on both the PC and the TV. It even allowed me to select a slightly wider resolution of 4096x2160.

The Google TV ecosystem works well and includes a useful Gemini AI integration that allows you to ask questions or play content via voice commands. Apple AirPlay casting works smoothly, though casting a photo automatically triggers the Dolby Vision profile, which alters the colors slightly compared to how they look on a mobile screen. The CEC functionality works beautifully; when I plugged a Fire TV stick into HDMI 1, the included Google remote and my phone's virtual remote natively controlled the Fire TV OS without any extra configuration. My only minor complaint is that controlling or waking the TV natively from a phone requires digging into the settings to ensure the TV stays in a standby state rather than fully shutting down.

💰 Price:

This TV is definitely not cheap, but you absolutely get what you pay for. It represents a high-end investment, and it is entirely worth the price if you have the budget for it.

🏆 Overall:

This is an exceptional, high-end, "end-game" TV that I highly recommend. It pairs a stunning high-refresh-rate display with a powerful built-in audio system that saves you from having to shell out extra money for a separate soundbar.

Pros:

Incredible picture quality with true blacks

Powerful, bass-rich built-in Dolby Atmos audio

Overdelivers on refresh rates (up to 180Hz at 4K and 330Hz at 1440p)

Premium, heavy-duty stand and backlit remote

Excellent smart features and seamless cross-platform remote compatibility

Cons:

Screen is still quite reflective when displaying a purely black screen

The chassis is notably thick

Native mobile wake-up features are turned off by default

In reality there was no halo or glare outside the white circle and the black background was perfectly black.

The image handling was okay. There certainly was more artifact especially on dark or grey scenes when you could sort of see the "blockyness" compared to my other one.   But sometimes this is the app itself like youtube on the television and not the image processing. The viewing angles were also decent even when looked at from an angle far to the side.

Sound is probably the weakest part of it. despite boasting that it has this amazing tuning by a reputable company and even has a visible subwoofer on the back, the sound is bad. I played the exact same song on this and my other tv, and the other one which is by no means known for having good audio absolutely destroyed this unit. That is not the biggest issue though honestly. If you are buying any television let alone a flagship everyone knows buy your own separate sound system.

Overall I do recommend this television. It does have many good strengths like the customization of almost all video and sound. the playback is excellent and you can easily watch your own catalogue on a usb. The brightness is outstanding for people who really care about nits. The only issue is two things.The sound as i mentioned but that is bascially an issue on all televisions. But also the fact you can get last years flagship OLED tv for a similar price or much cheaper. That besides in one category (brightness) based on my testing of my own television (a model 4 years older the newer oled) will honestly be better in almost every way. I think Hisense needs to slightly adjust the pricing for this to be a super compelling offer. But still is a strong television overall and okay value

title: Absolutely fantastic TV with premium gaming features, sharp display and vibrant colors.
body:
This is an incredible television! This is one of Hisense’s flagship models for this year, so it is priced accordingly, and it is packed with tons of features.

The first thing to note is that this TV is HEAVY. It is also far from being a thin design, with a massive 2 inches of thickness! The TV is over 65 lbs., likely requiring two people for setup. The base of the TV is not attached by default, so you will need to assemble and attach it to the TV. Once installed, the base holds the TV very well, keeping it solid and secure.

The frame is pretty much bezel free, despite the thickness and overall heft, making the screen look huge in my living room.

The build quality is excellent with thick plastics and a heavy construction that feels very premium. The plastics are all a matte colored black that is non-glossy and does not retain any fingerprints, though it does collect dust pretty quickly.

This is a Google TV. The interface is user friendly and easy to use. I found the entire UI on this TV to be extremely snappy and precise with no input delay on the remote. This is one of the fastest TV’s I’ve ever used when switching between apps or opening streaming services.

It has 3 HDMI inputs, one of which is ARC for my surround sound. The TV recognized my surround system system on its own and set all of the settings accordingly without me having to do anything.

Setup was very simple and I find the menus and settings interface to be simple and easy to navigate.

You can look up recommended calibration settings for this TV on Google to get the most out of the image quality, but I found that only a few minor tweaks were required, as the TV looks pretty darn fantastic right out of the box with the factory settings.

This is probably the closest TV I’ve used to an OLED without being an OLED. The mini LED bulbs that power this panel are extremely bright, producing up to 5,000 nits, for true HDR content. It pops with color, even at the 50% default setting with lots of vibrant details. 4K content when streaming looks fantastic and its upscaling for older content does a good job at reducing fuzziness.

For gaming, the refresh rate is incredibly fast at 180 hz native. Motion blur is completely non-existent in this TV, and when playing games at 60fps on my PS5 pro, I was blown away. This is far and beyond anything I have ever gamed on in my life. It will automatically switch to low latency mode and game mode when switching over to a game console. This TV practically does everything for you on its own.

I do recommend customizing / tweaking the game mode picture when playing on a console as it appears quite dim / dark by default and lacks a bit of vibrancy. It also does not have gsync enabled by default, so make sure to enable it through the TV settings when on game mode to get the fastest refresh rate when playing on PS5 / Pro.

Overall, a fantastic piece of equipment for streaming content, but really excels in gaming. It is clear that this TV was built with gaming in mind and it will likely hold up for the next 10 years due to the advanced features it has by default.

There are also built-in surround sound style TV speakers with dual mini-subs and upfiring speakers. While they sound pretty good for TV speakers, they lack in bass and do not have room filling sound. I would recommend upgrading to a proper 5.1 / 7.1 or Atmos system if you want to experience the most out of this TV.

title: The next generation in picture quality, contrast, brightness and color accuracy
body:
I have been enjoying a 65" Hisense ULED (Quantum Dot) TV for a few years now, and I thought the colors and brightness were excellent. This new Hisense 65UR9SG-series RGB Mini-LED takes the picture quality to another level. It is a incredible upgrade from the previous generation Hisense TVs.

The TV weighs approximately 28 kg with the stand, but I mounted mine on the wall. The stand is very heavy and sturdy so stability will not be an issue if the panel will be placed on a TV bench. I was able to reuse my existing wall-mounting bracket from the Hisense ULED TV. However, the screw holes on the UR9 are not the same height and distance as the old TV. This meant that the UR9 sat too low so I had to raise the wall bracket to ensure that the TV does not sit behind my center speaker. Mini-LED TVs are thicker than the older ULED TVs but it is not an issue because the UR9 comes with great 4.1.2 speakers. My home theater setup includes a Sony STR-DN1080 home theater receiver but I still tested the built-in speakers of the Hisense TV and they are surprisingly good. The voices are clear and centered, while ambient sounds have a wide sound stage. The speakers will not replace a home theater receiver but they are more than adequate.

The TV comes with a backlit remote control. The remote has a quality feel to it, with solid button presses and a backlight that comes on automatically when I pick up the remote. There are the standard shortcuts for streaming services, a circle navigation button and the usual volume and channel controls. There is a dedicated Input selection button but the TV automatically detects when a device is connected to an input (for example when powering up a video game console) so it rarely gets used in my setup.

The TV runs on Google TV, which boots quite fast and has a convenient home page. If you are familiar with Android TV, then Google TV has a similar interface. It is compatible with Alexa, Apple HomeKit and more for full integration in a home automation setup. Bluetooth 5.4 connectivity is also available to pair wireless keyboards and headphones. This really is a full-featured TV. Most important is the picture quality, and this is where the TV really shines.

RGB Mini-LED is the latest technology to compete with OLED TVs. This Hisense TV has native 180Hz, VRR, a peak brightness up to 5000 nits, 1056 local dimming zones and support for all of the HDR formats including Dolby Vision, Dolby Vision IQ, HDR10+ and more. There are so many options for configuring the picture to your liking, including a number of AI-based autoconfigurations and more advanced calibration menus. There are controls for the dimming/contrast, brightness, color, clarity and AI enhancements. I typically disable most of the picture enhancing features however the AI control of the contrast works quite well and brings more color depth during sports. Normally I setup my TVs with a Warm color temperature, but I got the best results using the "Standard" setting, with Color set to 60, and Hue left at the default setting, and brightness set to 80. I did disable all of the motion settings, and there is absolutely no motion blur whatsoever. The most visible upgrade compared to my older ULED TV is the incredible contrast and range of color. The deep black and super bright white allows the colors to pop without blooming or harshness. There is much more depth in color, with perfect skin tones and extremely detailed, dark scenes. I keep getting surprised at how good this TV looks regardless of what is playing (sports, gaming or movies). Everything seems much more natural because of the sharp contrast and brightness.

This Hisense UR9SG TV is an excellent upgrade in picture quality over my previous ULED TV. It offers the latest in home automation connectivity, numerous picture settings and absolutely stunning color and contrast depth. Very highly recommend this Hisense TV!

title: Thing of beauty
body:
I got this tv for our living room as I decided to upgrade. I had just recently purchased a smaller and much cheaper tv from Hisense and saw this as a chance to move the smaller tv to the basement and also see what difference there is between a cheaper tv and this "latest and greatest" tv.

I guess the very first thing anyone wants to know when buying a tv is, how does it look? Well I thought the picture on our cheaper tv was very good, but this UR9SG model tv is pretty spectacular. The colors are extremely vivid, the blacks are black as night, and the clarity in motion scenes is fantastic. Picture wise, this is like nothing I have ever seen. As for sound, it is much better than our cheaper tv. It looks like it has small built in subwoofers on the back, and although it won't compare to a good home theatre system, it does sound very good for a television. It will also crank up very loud, if loud music videos or movies is pleasing to you.

As for controls, they are very intuitive and easy, although there are a multitude of menus you spend a great deal of time scrolling through if you wish. There is also voice assist, although I just used the remote for setup. Speaking of the remote, it has buttons that respond nicely with no false or missed clicks that I noticed. It is also backlit so it's easy to use in the dark, and it is also voice capable if don't want to push buttons at all. It also looks kinda classy with it's construction and finish. Batteries are included.

There is plenty of connectivity on this tv, both wired and wireless. I won't go through them all - I think anything you might want to connect, and maybe lots of things you don't want to connect, will connect to this tv.

Which brings me to Google. If you are totally immersed in the Google connected smart sphere, then tv is definitely your dream tv. It does it all, and then does more. If your life is not totally intertwined with all things Google, you will likely find this tv frustrating and intrusive at first. Once you jump through the Google hoops, everything works as it should. But if by chance you don't already have a Google account, you are going to have to get one, because this tv won't operate without one. I was tempted to remove a star just for that reason, but I decided if you actually bought a Google tv, you probably have a Google account, or don't mind getting one.

In conclusion, would I recommend this tv? If it is in your budget, and you like the Google experience, then I can't see how you would be disappointed with this model. It's a beautiful, functional, and very high tech television. Even the remote is a notch above your typical cheap plastic remote. I can't think of anything I can criticize other than this is a pricey tv and not in everyone's budget.

title: One of the easiest TVs to setup to get great picture quality
body:
I got this TV for our guest bedroom because it provides the latest in video formats while providing excellent picture quality. The QD6 series from Hisense is part of their Hi-QLED range. I have always appreciated the beautiful, vivid colors of Hisense QLED TVs, and this one is no exception. It provides 4K Ultra HD resolution and upscaling, native 60Hz with 120 motion rate processing, Dolby Vision and HDR10+ support and more. I have the TV sitting on top of a bedroom dresser, so its very thin profile and small stand fit perfectly while ensuring stability. This TV is very light at just 12.2 kg. I got the 50" version as it is the perfect size for our guest room.

One of my favorite aspects of this TV is that it runs on Fire OS. I have Fire TV sticks for my other TVs, so setting this one up was simply a matter of logging in with my Amazon account. It automatically configures WiFi and even downloads the same apps that I have on my other Fire TV devices. The TV got a couple of firmware updates as well as the remote control when I first set it up. It was seamless and only took a few minutes. The remote is basically a Fire TV stick remote with some extra buttons for settings and inputs. The one thing that really stood out on this TV, even compared to other Hisense TVs, was how quick I was able to dial in a great picture. Selecting Filmmaker mode looked great, and I simply enabled Dynamic Contrast and Dynamic Color to High, set sharpness to the center value (50), and disabled any of the motion processing. Immediately I found the color temperature to be perfect (not too warm, and not too cool), the skin tones were natural, the brightness was punchy without blooming and the colors were vivid without blooming either. The contrast was very good, giving the picture a natural look where blacks were dark without crush or much grey. I did have to configure each input type manually as not all types (like SDR compared to HDR10) have the same picture settings available. There are more advanced settings to really dial in the screen but I really did not have to tweak anything at that level. The menus are responsive and very simple to use, especially if you are already familiar with Fire OS. I find the interface is similar to other TV operating systems so it is quick to navigate to your favorite streaming app from the menu, or just press the button on the remote for the dedicated apps. Normally I will always recommend a sound bar or full home theater setup, but the speakers on this TV are fine for basic, everyday use. Voices are clear but there is not much bass. There are 3 HDMI inputs (all support 4K 60Hz), a digital optical out, two USB ports, an antenna input and even an Ethernet port. This TV also has a Game Mode to reduce input lag, but keep in mind that it only supports up to 60Hz.

For our use as a guest room TV, this Hisense QD6 is an excellent addition to the room. I really appreciated how fast and simple it was to configure a great looking picture while Fire OS allowed me to instantly set up this TV to match my other Fire OS devices. Very highly recommend it!

title: 75" in the bedroom was a gamble. Pretty sure I won.
body:
Moved this into the master after years of a 55" that I kept squinting at from the bed. Setup was easy enough with two people. It’s big on a dresser, better on the wall. Once it’s up you stop noticing the frame and just notice the picture.

I left it in Filmmaker for movies and bumped brightness a bit for daytime. HDR is the part that sold me. Highlights actually pop instead of looking washed, and dark scenes stay dark without that grey haze my last TV had. Mini-LED dimming is doing the work there. Colours look rich on Netflix and Prime without going neon. Dolby Vision on the stuff that supports it is the cleanest I’ve had in this room.

144Hz is overkill for falling asleep to a show, but I game a bit on weekends and motion stays smooth. Google TV found all the apps in about two minutes. Voice remote is fine. Home screen ads are still annoying. That’s Google, not TCL.

Speakers are better than most TVs. Bang & Olufsen badge isn’t marketing fluff at normal volume. Dialogue is clear from the bed. I wouldn’t skip a soundbar forever if you watch action loud, but at night I don’t need one.

Only knock: the panel picks up lamp glare if you’ve got lights behind you. Close the blinds or shift the lamp and it’s gone.

For a bedroom this size is indulgent and I don’t care. Picture is the reason. If they made the 55 feel small, this is the one.

title: Old tv was from 2016, this a massive upgrade
body:
Had an LG from 2016, which was discontinued in 2017 (dang it). Didn't realize I was using broken software for almost 10 years (hdr settings were always choppy). Needless to say the upgrade to this 65" Hisense is an eye opener (literally, lol). Physically it looks better than my previous (no large grey plastic edges) and has better port locations (previous tvs ports location caused cables to bend at 90 degrees, broken a few). The software interface actually looks great (previous tv couldn't launch smart features anymore) and apps are easy to install. Easily connected to my Google account and integrated all my account settings without issues (YouTube settings, disney plus profiles, etc). I have it connected to a Lenovo Legion desktop running a RTX 5070 with 64gb of ram. First game I played on the Hisense tv was Stellar Blade. Was able to run at 165hz with no issues, looked ridiculous (details everywhere, background was clear, Eve's ponytail flowed like water, and I was able to actually block, thought I was just old, lol). I next tried Battlefield 6 and this is when smart features took over and picture automatically switched to HDR10+ (awesome no need to constantly look to the best options). Again game looked ridiculous, my accuracy went when wwwaaayyy up. I then watched a few older CGI movies to see how the tv would handle them (Starship Troppers Invasion 1080p, Appleseed 1080p, and Final Fantasy VII Advent Children 2160p 4K). Didn't notice much difference with Staship, the Hisense did a great job cleaning up the picture. Appleseed is where I started to see what the Hisense 65" Hi-QLED could do. The tv thought movie was a game and ran it with game settings. All the colors absolutely popped, the Ai features added details to skin and metal. Then Advent Children is where I noticed a huge difference. All the clothing in the movie had added texture and lighting, skin absorbed light properly (no shiny foreheads, lol), and details were highlighted in a way that made the experience seem like a different movie (context, watched Advent Children everyday for a year leading up to the release of FFVII Remake). The settings interface is a little clunky and some options seem like there in the wrong category, but that's a personal choice. Sound options are great, both Atmos and DTX, switches automatically depending on what is being viewed. Connected to 5.1 home theater through ARC and tv now controls home theater (volume up and down, but no other options available) with no sound lag to be heard. Light up buttons on tv remote is a handy feature. I highly recommend this tv, especially if it's on sale, especially if you're looking to upgrade from a 10 year old tv.

title: Great TV, bad customer service
body: I purchased the 75-inch Hisense U7SG during the Prime Day deal for $999. Unfortunately, after unboxing the brand-new TV, I discovered multiple dead/stuck pixels on the panel. I contacted both Amazon and Hisense, but neither has been willing to offer a replacement. Amazon’s only option is to return the TV for a refund, which puts me in a difficult position because the same TV is now selling for around $1,999. Hisense also opened a support case, and I even escalated it to Tier 2 support, but so far they do not seem to consider the visible pixel defects significant enough to justify a replacement. As a Lead Quality Engineer myself (although in the software field), I find this extremely disappointing. A brand-new premium TV should not arrive with visible panel defects, and I would expect the manufacturer to stand behind the quality of its product (especially when the issue was present right out of the box). What makes this even more frustrating is that I actually think the U7SG is an excellent TV. The picture quality, features, and especially the gaming capabilities are impressive. I was seriously considering Hisense for future TV purchases as well. Unfortunately, this experience with their quality assurance and customer support has completely changed my opinion. For comparison, I previously had a similar panel issue with an LG C5 OLED purchased from Best Buy. The TV was replaced immediately with a brand-new unit, and the replacement had no panel issues. I understand that manufacturers may have pixel policies and tolerances, but visible dead/stuck pixels on a brand-new TV should still be considered a defect. If this is now considered “acceptable” panel quality, that’s very disappointing. A great TV is only as good as the company standing behind it when something goes wrong.

body: Day 1 - Amazon delivery did great. Arrived on time, took away the boxes. Picture was great. All good. Day 3 - The TV stopped working. Power light is on, but no picture or response using the remote or the single button on the TV. Called Tech support, got an AI, worked through until they suggested uploading a new firmware version, went to the site as instructed and the form would not take my serial number to get the download. Called a different number got a live person who asked a few questions said they would have to send out a tech once they received my proof of purchase and a picture of the serial number and manufacturing date from the back of the TV. I have to get a buddy over to help lift it off the wall mount in the morning (76 lbs and 74 inches horizontally) and send the photos back to them so they can queue up a tech. Overall, not a good introduction to the Hisense line. I'll post more here as next steps are taken. Day 5 - Submitted picture of serial number and model # from back of TV Day 7 - Opened a chat with Hisense support. The case with my info had not been updated. They updated and released the ticket to a service rep. I was told it would be reviewed and a tech would get back to me within 24 to 48 hours to schedule a call. More to come. Last Update - Day 12 - Hisense customer service called and said the part was backordered and told me to return the TV to Amazon. Contrary to what I was told previously, they now said the earlier committed to "ship date" (which I verified twice with two different agent at Hisense) was in reality a part order date. The part now identified as backordered (on a TV produced in May of 2026) and to return the TV. Amazon has been amazing on the return.
