title: Impressive!
body:
I have quite a few TV’s around the house including OLED’s, UST projectors, and mini LED’s as well. Since two of my LED’s are this years’ models, I will be referencing those during this review. I will definitely compare the black levels of this Hisense to the OLED quality, but I will mainly focus on the newer mini LED’s.

The lineup:

Samsung M70H 65” On sale for $700 right now (https://www.amazon.ca/dp/B0GSC9VN3Y)

Hisense 75U7SF 75” $2000 (https://www.amazon.ca/dp/B0GJ1958F8)

Hisense UR8 55” $1500 (this one)

Black Levels

While these may not be OLED’s, they all do a pretty good job with black levels. Of course they can’t produce the same deep blacks as an OLED, but it is surprising at how far mini LED’s have come. As expected the less expensive M70 is the worst performing of the bunch, but it still does an excellent job for the price. It suffers from some light bleed on the bottom/top, but overall, if you are looking for a decent TV and don’t need top performance, this is a good choice. The U7 and the UR8 are pretty close, but I do have to give the edge to the UR8. The U7 has just a bit of light bleed on the bottom black bar, but only on the most demanding scenes. In fact, through all my testing I really only noticed it when I was a bit off angle and during specific scenes. One example would be Furiosa from the 17:26-24:45 mark, where it has a high red saturation and I noticed it a bit on the bottom. The UR8 on the other hand did not have this issue when I played the exact same scene. The M70 struggles with most scenes, but it still does a decent job and it is not that noticeable unless, like me, you are really looking for it. All handled shadow detail well, but both Hisense were noticeably better than the Samsung. For reference, I found The Dark Knight and The Batman looked great on all three, but the M70 was the weakest while the two Hisense were pretty much a tie.

Colour/Brightness/Refresh

All three did an excellent job with colour with the M70 coming in last, but not by too much. However, I have to say when I first tried The Watchmen on the UR8, I was pleasantly surprised at how much the colours actually popped compared to the U7. Again this movie looked pretty great on all three, but I am definitely giving the edge to the UR8 for colour reproduction. Brightness was definitely a non issue on each, but the UR8 with 5000 nits was the brightest. Finally, the refresh rates are higher on the more expensive models with the UR8 at 180Hz, U7 at 165Hz, and the Samsung at only 60Hz. While watching sports, I did find the Hisense TV’s did a better job, but the M70 was fine and the slower refresh rate didn’t really bother me all that much. Sorry, but I didn’t do any game testing on any of them.

Sound

I use a 7.2 system for my dedicated home theatre and sound bars for everything else, but I have to say, these companies have done wonders with integrated sound. Again the Samsung is the weakest here and both the U7/UR8 do an excellent job. In fact, they do such a good job, I would daresay you can probably get by without purchasing a sound bar.

Remotes/Stands/Reflection

While the Samsung remote is compact, I prefer both remotes (which are identical) on the Hisense models. All do a great job, but I like the full size version that comes with the Hisense TV’s. I also like the pedestal stands on both Hisense models better since you have more placement options. While they are a bit more difficult to put on, they are heavy “dutier” than the Samsung which has the wide leg design. Both the M70 and UR8 are more reflective than the U7 since it has a matte screen. Even though the UR8 says it has an anti-reflective screen, I found it reflected more light than my U7. Again, the Samsung was the most reflective and even though it is an often discussed topic (dislike of the matte screen), I found the U7 did a great job and there was little degradation in picture quality. This really comes down to personal preference and TV placement (living room vs. dedicated home theatre), so do some research if you are unsure.

Overall, the UR8 is a fantastic television. The colours really pop with the RGB mini LED’s and it does a fantastic job with black levels/shadow details. However, for $500 less (75”), the U7 is a strong contender. On the other hand, if you are looking to save some money and don’t need the deep blacks or high refresh rates, the M70 at $1100 (75”) is a great TV. Just don’t expect it to look as good as the other two. Hopefully I have touched on everything and made your choice a bit easier, depending on your needs. No matter which one you go for, I think you’ll be happy if that’s any help.

Recommended

Good luck with your decision/purchase

Sound is fine for news and sitcoms. Bang & Olufsen on the box made me think it would fill the room. It doesn’t. Fine until you turn it up, then it gets thin. I’ll add a soundbar later.

Only real annoyance is the screen. If you’ve got a window behind the couch you’ll see yourself in it during the day. Also the Google TV ads on the home screen get old fast.

Would I buy it again? For a basement or a room that can actually take a 98", yes. Just don’t pretend this is a normal TV. It’s a piece of furniture that happens to play hockey.

title: Sony's Bravia 3 II, A great set, but .....
body: If you're replacing the TV in your Home Theater System with a Dolby Vision capable one like this do yourself a favor and even if your HDMI cables are only a few years old, replace them all with Certified Ultra High Speed ones. Then unless you're an expert on both this TV and your A/V receiver, pay a technician to set it up for you. You will save about half of what life you have remaing in telephone time talking with tech support at Sony and tech support at your receivers manufacturer. This is no joke. Also make sure you have a verified source of a pure Dolby Vision signal, as many streaming services like Roku, transcode Dolby Vision to HDR10. So just because you're paying full price for a service like Paramount+ through Roku's Roku Channel don't expect to get a Dolby Vision signal. It can be done, but you have to know how. As for the TV itself, it's a magnificent piece of technology for the price. Once you're getting a proper signal and the inner settings are adjusted properly, the picture is stunning. Even the TV audio played through the TV's own speakers is impressive for TV speakers, but pump it through your HTS and it's fantastic, once the inner settings are correctly adjusted. All together, when set up properly it's a wonderful set, but do yourself a favor and pay for new cables and a tech to adjust it properly. It's worth it just to avoid a massive headache and frustration. It's a great set, just not "plug 'n' play."

body:
This review is more about Amazon and Amazon Warehouse. Amazon really needs to do a better job with its warehouse inspection process.

I received this Sony 43 Inch BRAVIA 2 II LED 4K HDR Smart Google TV that was clearly already damaged before it was shipped to me. As you can see in the photos, this is the condition it arrived in. On top of that, the bottom foam protector, which is supposed to help protect the TV during shipping, was already missing.

It is clear that the TV was not properly inspected before being sent out. Now, I have to go through the inconvenience of shipping the damaged TV back just to get my money refunded. This could have easily been avoided if Amazon had properly inspected the item before shipping it.

I want to make it clear that I have no issues with Sony. I love Sony products and am actually a loyal customer—I already have a 75-inch Sony TV in my living room. My frustration is entirely with Amazon Warehouse and how this item was handled.

I sincerely hope Sony sees this review and communicates with Amazon about situations like this. Experiences like this do not reflect well on Sony and can negatively affect loyal customers who trust and continue to purchase Sony products.

title: Sony's Bravia 3 II, A great set, but .....
body: If you're replacing the TV in your Home Theater System with a Dolby Vision capable one like this do yourself a favor and even if your HDMI cables are only a few years old, replace them all with Certified Ultra High Speed ones. Then unless you're an expert on both this TV and your A/V receiver, pay a technician to set it up for you. You will save about half of what life you have remaing in telephone time talking with tech support at Sony and tech support at your receivers manufacturer. This is no joke. Also make sure you have a verified source of a pure Dolby Vision signal, as many streaming services like Roku, transcode Dolby Vision to HDR10. So just because you're paying full price for a service like Paramount+ through Roku's Roku Channel don't expect to get a Dolby Vision signal. It can be done, but you have to know how. As for the TV itself, it's a magnificent piece of technology for the price. Once you're getting a proper signal and the inner settings are adjusted properly, the picture is stunning. Even the TV audio played through the TV's own speakers is impressive for TV speakers, but pump it through your HTS and it's fantastic, once the inner settings are correctly adjusted. All together, when set up properly it's a wonderful set, but do yourself a favor and pay for new cables and a tech to adjust it properly. It's worth it just to avoid a massive headache and frustration. It's a great set, just not "plug 'n' play."

At first I thought there was another protective layer of film on it that needed to be removed, but I quickly discovered that wasn't the case... This thing runs really hot too. It radiates a good bit of heat while in use. I was able to easily attach this to a rolling cart's mounting brackets. I don't really use the smart features. title: Beautiful OLED picture and more capable than I expected
body:
Impressive TV with an amazing picture. After the initial setup and installing the apps I use, I went straight to YouTube. Interestingly, the #1 video it recommended was an "OLED 4K Demo" type video, and I was mesmerized by the picture quality. I can practically put my face up against this TV and it still looks good. The colors and clarity are brilliant, the blacks really are absolutely black to my eyes, and the picture is smooth and crisp.

I was also impressed that at least one popular 3D game could be installed directly on the TV as an app, with no console or PC. I connected my Bluetooth controller and played it directly on the TV. I wasn't expecting that. It looked like it was running at fairly minimal graphics quality, but it was playing and my controller worked.

This TV is very thin, and the instructions warn not to pinch the screen with your thumb when lifting it. I can see why. The back has a thicker section, but the screen becomes extremely thin at the edges, so I handled it carefully.

The picture and color quality look excellent even from a very side-angle view, and the sound quality is excellent too.

It comes with two small but sturdy legs that screw onto the bottom. With the legs installed, it feels stable.

Power use has also been pretty low in my setup. My backup battery reports about 40W-90W depending on how bright the picture is. A dark movie can hover around 40W, while a mostly white screen can approach 100W. Most movies I've watched hover around 60W, considerably less than my old TV used.

The remote is quite nice. I turned on Gemini mode in the TV settings, and I can press and hold the microphone button on the remote and speak naturally to it. It hears me clearly from across the room, and I can use my voice to run searches.

title: Ok, I get it. I now understand the OLED hype
body:
Our old 1080 TV in the master bedroom was in dire need of replacing. One of my friends had mentioned many times that switching to OLEDs made movie watching so much more immersive and special. I always kind of brushed it off over the top hyperbole.

I got this in and set up in the bedroom. Setup was dead simple. I just swapped over the cabling to our sound bar and network from our old TV into this and everything just worked. There was a quick initial firmware update that I let complete before starting to watch something. I was too anxious to see the picture quality and skipped over the calibration. I need to go back and do that still.

The initial images were as good as my friend had been telling me. When you hear "truly black blacks" you don't really comprehend it until you see it in person. The dark areas of the screen are a black hole of zero light. There is no bleed. The colors are bright and sharp against the deep inky blacks. We watched Project Hail Mary in 4K HDR IMAX and the spacewalk scenes were mind-blowing and sharp as a tack. We watched an F1 race this morning and the colors were vibrant and the crowds were made up of actual people instead of vaguely people-shaped objects.

I can't comment on the built-in GoogleTV bits as I just plugged my own Google Streamer and am using that exclusively for now. Same for the audio quality as we are using an external sound bar connected through the optical port.

What I realized very quickly was that this TV was going to cost me a lot of money. It'll do that by making me NEED to upgrade the 80" TV in our living room now. After watching movies on this 55" OLED I really don't want to go back to our old LED Sony TV. Pictures of a TV screen do the actual image no justice at all. You really just have to see it for yourself.

It would be like comparing a Mercedes E class to a C class.

As an entry level OLED TV, the Bravia 6 is actually quite outstanding. I'd recommend shelling out the extra couple hundred bucks for the Bravia 8 though. If not possible, this TV still provides an exceptional viewing experience for both movies and gaming. If anything, there are more hdmi 2.1 ports on this vs the Bravia 8 so you can plug in multiple gaming systems and achieve 4k 120hz for each one. title: Damaged TV Sent by Amazon Warehouse Poor Inspection Process
body:
This review is more about Amazon and Amazon Warehouse. Amazon really needs to do a better job with its warehouse inspection process.

I received this Sony 43 Inch BRAVIA 2 II LED 4K HDR Smart Google TV that was clearly already damaged before it was shipped to me. As you can see in the photos, this is the condition it arrived in. On top of that, the bottom foam protector, which is supposed to help protect the TV during shipping, was already missing.

It is clear that the TV was not properly inspected before being sent out. Now, I have to go through the inconvenience of shipping the damaged TV back just to get my money refunded. This could have easily been avoided if Amazon had properly inspected the item before shipping it.

I want to make it clear that I have no issues with Sony. I love Sony products and am actually a loyal customer—I already have a 75-inch Sony TV in my living room. My frustration is entirely with Amazon Warehouse and how this item was handled.

I sincerely hope Sony sees this review and communicates with Amazon about situations like this. Experiences like this do not reflect well on Sony and can negatively affect loyal customers who trust and continue to purchase Sony products.

Really? Setting the volume to 1 will ruin my ears? Worse: it will also frequently forget the audio output setting and switch to TV speakers instead of the audio system. I never want the TV speakers; that's why I have an audio system. Even worse: fairly frequently it will just drop the volume to zero as I'm watching a show or playing a game. The absolute worst: sometimes it will route the sound to BOTH the TV Speakers and the audio system at the same time. Switching between settings goes from silence on both, or sound from both. Occasionally, there will be no sound at all from EITHER output regardless of setting. Sometimes rebooting the TV will solve these issues (a hard reboot, not just turning the TV off/on), sometimes it persists until after multiple reboots. Watching TV should be a simple as turning the TV on, not spending minutes fiddling with trying to get the sound right. But not with this TV.

title: Beautiful OLED picture and more capable than I expected
body:
Impressive TV with an amazing picture. After the initial setup and installing the apps I use, I went straight to YouTube. Interestingly, the #1 video it recommended was an "OLED 4K Demo" type video, and I was mesmerized by the picture quality. I can practically put my face up against this TV and it still looks good. The colors and clarity are brilliant, the blacks really are absolutely black to my eyes, and the picture is smooth and crisp.

I was also impressed that at least one popular 3D game could be installed directly on the TV as an app, with no console or PC. I connected my Bluetooth controller and played it directly on the TV. I wasn't expecting that. It looked like it was running at fairly minimal graphics quality, but it was playing and my controller worked.

This TV is very thin, and the instructions warn not to pinch the screen with your thumb when lifting it. I can see why. The back has a thicker section, but the screen becomes extremely thin at the edges, so I handled it carefully.

The picture and color quality look excellent even from a very side-angle view, and the sound quality is excellent too.

It comes with two small but sturdy legs that screw onto the bottom. With the legs installed, it feels stable.

Power use has also been pretty low in my setup. My backup battery reports about 40W-90W depending on how bright the picture is. A dark movie can hover around 40W, while a mostly white screen can approach 100W. Most movies I've watched hover around 60W, considerably less than my old TV used.

The remote is quite nice. I turned on Gemini mode in the TV settings, and I can press and hold the microphone button on the remote and speak naturally to it. It hears me clearly from across the room, and I can use my voice to run searches.

title: Ok, I get it. I now understand the OLED hype
body:
Our old 1080 TV in the master bedroom was in dire need of replacing. One of my friends had mentioned many times that switching to OLEDs made movie watching so much more immersive and special. I always kind of brushed it off over the top hyperbole.

I got this in and set up in the bedroom. Setup was dead simple. I just swapped over the cabling to our sound bar and network from our old TV into this and everything just worked. There was a quick initial firmware update that I let complete before starting to watch something. I was too anxious to see the picture quality and skipped over the calibration. I need to go back and do that still.

The initial images were as good as my friend had been telling me. When you hear "truly black blacks" you don't really comprehend it until you see it in person. The dark areas of the screen are a black hole of zero light. There is no bleed. The colors are bright and sharp against the deep inky blacks. We watched Project Hail Mary in 4K HDR IMAX and the spacewalk scenes were mind-blowing and sharp as a tack. We watched an F1 race this morning and the colors were vibrant and the crowds were made up of actual people instead of vaguely people-shaped objects.

I can't comment on the built-in GoogleTV bits as I just plugged my own Google Streamer and am using that exclusively for now. Same for the audio quality as we are using an external sound bar connected through the optical port.

What I realized very quickly was that this TV was going to cost me a lot of money. It'll do that by making me NEED to upgrade the 80" TV in our living room now. After watching movies on this 55" OLED I really don't want to go back to our old LED Sony TV. Pictures of a TV screen do the actual image no justice at all. You really just have to see it for yourself.

title: Entry level OLED
body:
At first I was confused why this Bravia 6 was released years later after the Bravia 8, thinking the Bravia 8 was the newer TV. But in fact this Bravia 6 is the newest TV in Sony's lineup. However, its performance is actually not as great as the older Bravia 8 or the LG G4 I currently have from 2 years ago. This made me think of reviewing this as a 4 star TV, but then I realized this is actually an entry level OLED TV, not a premium one with a higher price tag. It would be like comparing a Mercedes E class to a C class.

As an entry level OLED TV, the Bravia 6 is actually quite outstanding. I'd recommend shelling out the extra couple hundred bucks for the Bravia 8 though. If not possible, this TV still provides an exceptional viewing experience for both movies and gaming. If anything, there are more hdmi 2.1 ports on this vs the Bravia 8 so you can plug in multiple gaming systems and achieve 4k 120hz for each one. Not only that, you still get dolby vision, hdr 10, and atmos support. So you actually can't go wrong with this TV even though it lacks some premium features that the Bravia 8 has, like having the entire screen function as a speaker.

title: Damaged TV Sent by Amazon Warehouse Poor Inspection Process
body:
This review is more about Amazon and Amazon Warehouse. Amazon really needs to do a better job with its warehouse inspection process.

I received this Sony 43 Inch BRAVIA 2 II LED 4K HDR Smart Google TV that was clearly already damaged before it was shipped to me. As you can see in the photos, this is the condition it arrived in. On top of that, the bottom foam protector, which is supposed to help protect the TV during shipping, was already missing.

It is clear that the TV was not properly inspected before being sent out. Now, I have to go through the inconvenience of shipping the damaged TV back just to get my money refunded. This could have easily been avoided if Amazon had properly inspected the item before shipping it.

I want to make it clear that I have no issues with Sony. I love Sony products and am actually a loyal customer—I already have a 75-inch Sony TV in my living room. My frustration is entirely with Amazon Warehouse and how this item was handled.

I sincerely hope Sony sees this review and communicates with Amazon about situations like this. Experiences like this do not reflect well on Sony and can negatively affect loyal customers who trust and continue to purchase Sony products.

body: Two stars because the picture quality is fine, but the sounds handling on this TV is anything BUT fine. Firstly, it will not remember the volume setting. Next: any attempt to move the volume from zero is met with a dialog that must be dismissed announcing that running the volume at elevated levels could injure your hearing. Every. Single. Time. Really? Setting the volume to 1 will ruin my ears? Worse: it will also frequently forget the audio output setting and switch to TV speakers instead of the audio system. I never want the TV speakers; that's why I have an audio system. Even worse: fairly frequently it will just drop the volume to zero as I'm watching a show or playing a game. The absolute worst: sometimes it will route the sound to BOTH the TV Speakers and the audio system at the same time. Switching between settings goes from silence on both, or sound from both. Occasionally, there will be no sound at all from EITHER output regardless of setting. Sometimes rebooting the TV will solve these issues (a hard reboot, not just turning the TV off/on), sometimes it persists until after multiple reboots. Watching TV should be a simple as turning the TV on, not spending minutes fiddling with trying to get the sound right. But not with this TV.

title: Sony's Bravia 3 II, A great set, but .....
body: If you're replacing the TV in your Home Theater System with a Dolby Vision capable one like this do yourself a favor and even if your HDMI cables are only a few years old, replace them all with Certified Ultra High Speed ones. Then unless you're an expert on both this TV and your A/V receiver, pay a technician to set it up for you. You will save about half of what life you have remaing in telephone time talking with tech support at Sony and tech support at your receivers manufacturer. This is no joke. Also make sure you have a verified source of a pure Dolby Vision signal, as many streaming services like Roku, transcode Dolby Vision to HDR10. So just because you're paying full price for a service like Paramount+ through Roku's Roku Channel don't expect to get a Dolby Vision signal. It can be done, but you have to know how. As for the TV itself, it's a magnificent piece of technology for the price. Once you're getting a proper signal and the inner settings are adjusted properly, the picture is stunning. Even the TV audio played through the TV's own speakers is impressive for TV speakers, but pump it through your HTS and it's fantastic, once the inner settings are correctly adjusted. All together, when set up properly it's a wonderful set, but do yourself a favor and pay for new cables and a tech to adjust it properly. It's worth it just to avoid a massive headache and frustration. It's a great set, just not "plug 'n' play."

OLED definitely has the edge in pure picture quality, but this Mini LED still looks very good once properly tuned.

After 6 days of use and some tweaking to the picture and sound settings for my room, I’m really happy with it. For more than half the price of an OLED, it delivers solid performance. The bonus of 5 free movie credits and 100 free movies on the Sony Core app is a nice extra.

Great TV, fast delivery, and excellent packaging. I’m satisfied with my purchase and would recommend it.

title: Fantastic Quality Sony television with incredible 4K upscaling at a reasonable price
body: This TV is well worth the money with fantastic picture quality using my PS5, my Apple TV 4K, and the built-in google OS. The Dolby Vision HDR is impressive. The picture is very clear and vivid, even with settings turned down. I am quite impressed with the mini LED ability to deliver much deeper blacks in movies and games. It was super easy for me to set up. The legs (or feet) just slide right into their slots and click into place with no other hardware required to install them. I have mine connected to my fiber optic internet connection via cat 6 cable. The peripherals are connected via high speed HDMI cables. The built-in speakers have decent sound quality, better than I expected in my modest apartment. I may invest in a sound bar in the future for improved “surround” sound effects that take advantage of the Dolby Atmos audio. It powers on instantly and has ZERO lag time when operating, putting it MILES ahead of any fire tv set I’ve owned before it. I became tired of the 3-year shelf life of my old Insignia, as the back light quit suddenly. I was willing to invest in a better quality built Sony television that should last for many years longer, instead of throwing away a cheap television every few years, since electronic waste is fast becoming a major problem today. I’ve had great success with Sony TVs in the past, including my first 40 inch Bravia HD TV I bought back in 2005, which still works great today as a second tv in my bedroom. My only complaint is that only two of the four HDMI plugs are 2.1. You really do get what you pay for!

title: Beautiful OLED picture and more capable than I expected
body:
Impressive TV with an amazing picture. After the initial setup and installing the apps I use, I went straight to YouTube. Interestingly, the #1 video it recommended was an "OLED 4K Demo" type video, and I was mesmerized by the picture quality. I can practically put my face up against this TV and it still looks good. The colors and clarity are brilliant, the blacks really are absolutely black to my eyes, and the picture is smooth and crisp.

I was also impressed that at least one popular 3D game could be installed directly on the TV as an app, with no console or PC. I connected my Bluetooth controller and played it directly on the TV. I wasn't expecting that. It looked like it was running at fairly minimal graphics quality, but it was playing and my controller worked.

This TV is very thin, and the instructions warn not to pinch the screen with your thumb when lifting it. I can see why. The back has a thicker section, but the screen becomes extremely thin at the edges, so I handled it carefully.

The picture and color quality look excellent even from a very side-angle view, and the sound quality is excellent too.

It comes with two small but sturdy legs that screw onto the bottom. With the legs installed, it feels stable.

Power use has also been pretty low in my setup. My backup battery reports about 40W-90W depending on how bright the picture is. A dark movie can hover around 40W, while a mostly white screen can approach 100W. Most movies I've watched hover around 60W, considerably less than my old TV used.

The remote is quite nice. I turned on Gemini mode in the TV settings, and I can press and hold the microphone button on the remote and speak naturally to it. It hears me clearly from across the room, and I can use my voice to run searches.

title: Ok, I get it. I now understand the OLED hype
body:
Our old 1080 TV in the master bedroom was in dire need of replacing. One of my friends had mentioned many times that switching to OLEDs made movie watching so much more immersive and special. I always kind of brushed it off over the top hyperbole.

I got this in and set up in the bedroom. Setup was dead simple. I just swapped over the cabling to our sound bar and network from our old TV into this and everything just worked. There was a quick initial firmware update that I let complete before starting to watch something. I was too anxious to see the picture quality and skipped over the calibration. I need to go back and do that still.

The initial images were as good as my friend had been telling me. When you hear "truly black blacks" you don't really comprehend it until you see it in person. The dark areas of the screen are a black hole of zero light. There is no bleed. The colors are bright and sharp against the deep inky blacks. We watched Project Hail Mary in 4K HDR IMAX and the spacewalk scenes were mind-blowing and sharp as a tack. We watched an F1 race this morning and the colors were vibrant and the crowds were made up of actual people instead of vaguely people-shaped objects.

I can't comment on the built-in GoogleTV bits as I just plugged my own Google Streamer and am using that exclusively for now. Same for the audio quality as we are using an external sound bar connected through the optical port.

What I realized very quickly was that this TV was going to cost me a lot of money. It'll do that by making me NEED to upgrade the 80" TV in our living room now. After watching movies on this 55" OLED I really don't want to go back to our old LED Sony TV. Pictures of a TV screen do the actual image no justice at all. You really just have to see it for yourself.

It would be like comparing a Mercedes E class to a C class.

As an entry level OLED TV, the Bravia 6 is actually quite outstanding. I'd recommend shelling out the extra couple hundred bucks for the Bravia 8 though. If not possible, this TV still provides an exceptional viewing experience for both movies and gaming. If anything, there are more hdmi 2.1 ports on this vs the Bravia 8 so you can plug in multiple gaming systems and achieve 4k 120hz for each one. This review is more about Amazon and Amazon Warehouse. Amazon really needs to do a better job with its warehouse inspection process.

I want to make it clear that I have no issues with Sony. I love Sony products and am actually a loyal customer—I already have a 75-inch Sony TV in my living room. My frustration is entirely with Amazon Warehouse and how this item was handled.

I sincerely hope Sony sees this review and communicates with Amazon about situations like this. Experiences like this do not reflect well on Sony and can negatively affect loyal customers who trust and continue to purchase Sony products.

Every time the TV is turned on, it sets the volume to zero. If it was only that, it would just be annoying. But... Next: any attempt to move the volume from zero is met with a dialog that must be dismissed announcing that running the volume at elevated levels could injure your hearing. Every. Single. Time. Really? Setting the volume to 1 will ruin my ears? Worse: it will also frequently forget the audio output setting and switch to TV speakers instead of the audio system. I never want the TV speakers; that's why I have an audio system. Even worse: fairly frequently it will just drop the volume to zero as I'm watching a show or playing a game. The absolute worst: sometimes it will route the sound to BOTH the TV Speakers and the audio system at the same time. Switching between settings goes from silence on both, or sound from both. Occasionally, there will be no sound at all from EITHER output regardless of setting. Sometimes rebooting the TV will solve these issues (a hard reboot, not just turning the TV off/on), sometimes it persists until after multiple reboots. Watching TV should be a simple as turning the TV on, not spending minutes fiddling with trying to get the sound right. But not with this TV.

title: Sony's Bravia 3 II, A great set, but .....
body: If you're replacing the TV in your Home Theater System with a Dolby Vision capable one like this do yourself a favor and even if your HDMI cables are only a few years old, replace them all with Certified Ultra High Speed ones. Then unless you're an expert on both this TV and your A/V receiver, pay a technician to set it up for you. You will save about half of what life you have remaing in telephone time talking with tech support at Sony and tech support at your receivers manufacturer. This is no joke. Also make sure you have a verified source of a pure Dolby Vision signal, as many streaming services like Roku, transcode Dolby Vision to HDR10. So just because you're paying full price for a service like Paramount+ through Roku's Roku Channel don't expect to get a Dolby Vision signal. It can be done, but you have to know how. As for the TV itself, it's a magnificent piece of technology for the price. Once you're getting a proper signal and the inner settings are adjusted properly, the picture is stunning. Even the TV audio played through the TV's own speakers is impressive for TV speakers, but pump it through your HTS and it's fantastic, once the inner settings are correctly adjusted. All together, when set up properly it's a wonderful set, but do yourself a favor and pay for new cables and a tech to adjust it properly. It's worth it just to avoid a massive headache and frustration. It's a great set, just not "plug 'n' play."

title: Fantastic Quality Sony television with incredible 4K upscaling at a reasonable price
body: This TV is well worth the money with fantastic picture quality using my PS5, my Apple TV 4K, and the built-in google OS. The Dolby Vision HDR is impressive. The picture is very clear and vivid, even with settings turned down. I am quite impressed with the mini LED ability to deliver much deeper blacks in movies and games. It was super easy for me to set up. The legs (or feet) just slide right into their slots and click into place with no other hardware required to install them. I have mine connected to my fiber optic internet connection via cat 6 cable. The peripherals are connected via high speed HDMI cables. The built-in speakers have decent sound quality, better than I expected in my modest apartment. I may invest in a sound bar in the future for improved “surround” sound effects that take advantage of the Dolby Atmos audio. It powers on instantly and has ZERO lag time when operating, putting it MILES ahead of any fire tv set I’ve owned before it. I became tired of the 3-year shelf life of my old Insignia, as the back light quit suddenly. I was willing to invest in a better quality built Sony television that should last for many years longer, instead of throwing away a cheap television every few years, since electronic waste is fast becoming a major problem today. I’ve had great success with Sony TVs in the past, including my first 40 inch Bravia HD TV I bought back in 2005, which still works great today as a second tv in my bedroom. My only complaint is that only two of the four HDMI plugs are 2.1. You really do get what you pay for!

title: Extremely Disappointing Experience Streaming Issues, Poor Software, and Terrible Support
body:
I strongly do not recommend purchasing a Sony Bravia TV.

My experience with my 65-inch Sony Bravia has been extremely frustrating, especially when it comes to Netflix and general streaming performance. Streaming is consistently unreliable. Apps freeze, fail to load content properly, cut off unexpectedly, or simply do not work the way they should on a premium television. Watching Netflix or other streaming services has become a constant headache rather than an enjoyable experience.

Another major issue is the picture behaviour. The hue and colour tone appear to shift noticeably between changing scenes, which is distracting and makes the viewing experience feel inconsistent. For a brand that markets itself as premium, the software and image handling have been very disappointing.

The app experience is also glitchy and poorly optimized. Apps can lag, freeze, or display content incorrectly. The menu system is terribly laid out, unintuitive, and frustrating to navigate. Simple tasks take longer than they should, and the overall interface feels clunky.

Worst of all, Sony customer service has been practically nonexistent and completely unhelpful. When dealing with ongoing issues, support has not provided meaningful solutions or proper assistance. For a product at this price point, that level of service is unacceptable.

Overall, this TV has been one of the most disappointing electronics purchases I have made. Between the streaming problems, colour shifting, freezing apps, poor menu design, and lack of real customer support, I would strongly recommend avoiding Sony Bravia TVs.

title: Best TV I have ever owned, but it's not perfect
body: Overall, I have been very impressed with this television. It is by far the best TV I have ever owned. That said, there are a couple of things preventing me from giving this a full five-star rating. Here's a brief recap of my thoughts regarding this Sony 65 Inch Mini LED QLED 4K Ultra HD BRAVIA 9 TV Positives: 1. Brightest picture I have ever seen on a TV 2. Clearest, most detailed picture on any TV I have owned. Colors are accurate with no smearing 3. Metal feet instead of plastic 4. Initial setup is fairly simple even though Sony does not ship this set with an owners manual 5. The Bravia 9 can be connected to Alexa, Google Home, and Apple Home Kit devices, but I chose not to integrate those services 6. The Sony home interface is logical and well laid out. It is intuitive and easy to find what you're looking for 7. The sound system built into this set is superior to the standard sound of any other TV I have owned. You may not even care if you have a soundbar or receiver. The sound is that good. 8. Excellent remote. Backlit, charges via USB-C (just think how much you'll save on batteries!) and it also has a remote finding feature 9. Sony has figured out how to return to your last used source (most of the time) when you turn the TV on. That was a pet peeve of mine for the past ten to fifteen years of owning smart TVs. I used to have to click through two to six screens to return to my previous settings when I turned the TV on. Now, the TV goes directly to Hulu if that was the last source I was on when I turned the TV off. If we were watching Netflix, it goes to Netflix when we turn the TV on. It doesn't work every single day, but at least 5 or 6 days a week it does, and that's a big improvement. Huzzah! The less than positives: 1. No printed manual. I understand that most companies no longer give you a printed manual, but this is Sony's 2024 flagship TV. Something this expensive warrants a printed manual 2. Only two HDMI 2.1 ports. Every HDMI port should be a 4K port on the top TV that Sony offers 3. The HDMI ports are poorly positioned on the back of the TV. They are so close to the back panel of the TV that it is very difficult to plug HDMI cables in and out. See attached photo 4. There are no component or composite connections on the rear of the TV. Certainly, these are not connections that everyone needs these days, but backwards compatibility should be guaranteed on a flagship television. 5. The remote has a problem turning the set off consistently. At least every other day or so, I hit the power button to turn off the TV and nothing happens. I have to get out of my chair and walk towards the TV, pointing the remote at the sensor on the front of the TV before it will turn the thing off. It's annoying and frankly, it makes no sense because it's a Bluetooth remote. Line of sight should not be an issue at all. I am blaming this on the TV instead of the remote, because the remote is Bluetooth, not IR. So while this SONY Bravia 9 is absolutely the best TV I have ever owned, the odd decisions by the manufacturer to save a few cents with a flagship product prevent me from assigning a rating higher than four stars. It's not a great value compared to premier products from other companies, but it sure is an excellent TV.

title: Beautiful picture and great for gaming
body: 4/01/26 update: one small unuformity spot has formed in the lower left of the screen, but it's not super noticable. But a word of warning to people who plan to use an Xbox with Dolby Vision gaming and Dolby Atmos sound enabled. DO NOT buy this TV! There is a significant audio lag in games with those features enabled (i have tried different cables and every known suggestion). The only way to reduce the noticable lag is to turn off Dolby Vision for gaming and switch the sound from Dolby Atmos to something less like 5.1 (in Xbox settings). And that is one of the reasons I bought this TV. To use those features on a premium, new TV where I could run the Xbox straight to the TV instead of through a receiver and have native TV Dolby Atmos and Dolby Vision support. I replaced a 2016 Sony Z9D with this set. The B9 surpasses the Z9D in almost every area, with the notable exception of black levels and blooming (which the B9 was supposed to be incomparable at). The black levels and blooming were not an improvement over my Z9D (with any setting), but then again the Z9D had a superlative backlight drive and local dimming. The blooming/light bleed is actually significantly worse than my Z9D, despite what reviews have said. If there's a bright light or lamp behind a darker object, like someone's head, the light clearly bleeds into the darker space. However, overall brightness, picture processing, and gaming are outstanding. Gaming at 120hz is a true joy. title: Excellent picture; Poor Software; Substandard Tuner
body: If I could find a decent HDMI monitor without all the crappy “smart TV” stuff, I would buy it instead! But this TV does have a great picture and I figured I could just use it as an HDMI monitor since it has several HDMI inputs. That is what I have done for years with my previous 60” Sony TV. I wish Sony would dump Google. The Google software in this TV is about as unreliable as the rest of “modern” software. It's a consequence of the hap-hazard, undisciplined way all consumer software is now developed. We all know how MS Windows behaves unpredictably and often crashes. The plight of the Boeing 737 Max is an example of what happens when commercial “worst practices” creeps into what used to be the more disciplined way of developing software. First of all, be aware that this TV, like almost all newer software based products, does not come with a manual. So there is really no way of knowing where to find a particular option or even a way to know that an option might exist buried somewhere deep in the endless setup menus. Here is just one example: I want my TV to power up using a particular HDMI input every time it is turned on. After searching for at least half an hour, I found the option I needed to change the power up behavior. I set it to “Use last TV input”. Problem solved, right? Well sort of. This TV exhibits the same unpredictable behavior as almost every software based product out there. After choosing this option, this TV does indeed power up most the time to the HDMI input it was using when last turned off. But NOT ALL THE TIME. Every now and then, it insists on powering up to the “home screen” menu. It takes about 6 button pushes to get it back to using the input I want! There seems to be no logic to when it will power up to the home menu. Come on Sony, get your act together and develop some reliable software. Get rid of Google as a partner and make your software reliable! Besides the unpredictable software, this TV suffers from a weak tuner. My previous Sony tuned in my antenna with no issues. I have about 60 local channels to choose from. This tuner, using the exact same connection as the previous Sony TV, has many multi-path issues. It suffers from constant pixelization and dropouts. Like I said, I simply replaced the old TV with this one plugged into the exact same attic mounted antenna. So this tuner is of lower quality than my previous TV's tuner. Since I don't normally use the built in tuner, I have not yet experimented with booster amps etc. to try to get this TV to work right with my antenna. My TiVo over-the-air box with four built-in tuners tunes in my antenna with no problem! Something to be aware of if you plan to use the tuner instead of just the "smart" features and HDMI inputs.

title: The More Modern And Expensive, The Fewer Input/Output Options?
body: For my purposes this is the Burger King of TVs -- A Whopper. It is like a 3 by 5 card -- But, 3 feet by 5 feet. It weighs in at around 70 pounds yet is under 2 inches thick. For some unknown reason, as TVs have gotten larger, manufacturers have decreased the number and variety of inputs and outputs. Why? Don't they know people still have remote speakers, or other devices, which need analog sound sources, like from RCA, or even phone jacks? Or, that they might want to display video from devices which have composite, component or VGA outputs? (The Australian model of this TV is reported to have a headphone jack. Why not the US version?) Wireless, Bluetooth, digital and HDMI alone do not meet the needs of everyone. Nor is the expense, time, trouble involved in work-arounds like HDMI audio extractors and the like. This TV uses a VESA 300x300 mounting pattern. Meaning the mounting holes are in a square, 300 millimeters on a side. That's around 12 inches square which should be adequate. The mini-LED concept is said to rival QLED screens. The images on this TV do appear to be better than the ones produced by a six-year-old Sony 49 inch XBR950 Bravia. I dislike the limited variety of inputs and outputs especially on TVs in this price class. One would think more expensive TVs would have plenty of design leeway, and profit margin, to allow for the inclusion of a variety of inputs and outputs. Based on the 'acres' of empty space on the back of this TV, apparently that is not the case. This kind of thinking by TV manufacturers borders on criminal. The TV is good. Sony's limited input/output decision is for the birds.

title: OLED price, but not OLED quality

There are a lot of panels to attach to the rear of the TV and it is not clear to me what they are all for, but for the most part you don't need to care since most people get more enjoyment from the front of their TV than the rear, so put 'em on or don't. The TV is not light, so you will want a helper if you can get one. The feet for the TV can either be spaced wide apart or narrow to accommodate entertainment centers that aren't as wide as the TV. Mine was missing a rubber pad, though, which is disappointing for a product this expensive. The TV is alright. I would say it is better than any regular LCD screen I've had, but not astoundingly so. I think this is likely to be more durable than an OLED TV, too. If you're not using a sound bar or other external sound source, the TV's built in speakers are not half bad. (Far better than my Samsung, but nothing you'd write home about.) You can probably get better TVs for a similar price, but if there is a sale or it comes down in price relative to an OLED screen then it is superior to a budget LCD TV and worth considering in my opinion.

body:
This review is more about Amazon and Amazon Warehouse. Amazon really needs to do a better job with its warehouse inspection process.

I want to make it clear that I have no issues with Sony. I love Sony products and am actually a loyal customer—I already have a 75-inch Sony TV in my living room. My frustration is entirely with Amazon Warehouse and how this item was handled.

I sincerely hope Sony sees this review and communicates with Amazon about situations like this. Experiences like this do not reflect well on Sony and can negatively affect loyal customers who trust and continue to purchase Sony products.

Sometimes rebooting the TV will solve these issues (a hard reboot, not just turning the TV off/on), sometimes it persists until after multiple reboots. title: Sony's Bravia 3 II, A great set, but .....
body: If you're replacing the TV in your Home Theater System with a Dolby Vision capable one like this do yourself a favor and even if your HDMI cables are only a few years old, replace them all with Certified Ultra High Speed ones. Then unless you're an expert on both this TV and your A/V receiver, pay a technician to set it up for you. You will save about half of what life you have remaing in telephone time talking with tech support at Sony and tech support at your receivers manufacturer. This is no joke. Also make sure you have a verified source of a pure Dolby Vision signal, as many streaming services like Roku, transcode Dolby Vision to HDR10. So just because you're paying full price for a service like Paramount+ through Roku's Roku Channel don't expect to get a Dolby Vision signal. It can be done, but you have to know how. As for the TV itself, it's a magnificent piece of technology for the price. Once you're getting a proper signal and the inner settings are adjusted properly, the picture is stunning. Even the TV audio played through the TV's own speakers is impressive for TV speakers, but pump it through your HTS and it's fantastic, once the inner settings are correctly adjusted. All together, when set up properly it's a wonderful set, but do yourself a favor and pay for new cables and a tech to adjust it properly. It's worth it just to avoid a massive headache and frustration. It's a great set, just not "plug 'n' play."

title: Fantastic Quality Sony television with incredible 4K upscaling at a reasonable price
body: This TV is well worth the money with fantastic picture quality using my PS5, my Apple TV 4K, and the built-in google OS. The Dolby Vision HDR is impressive. The picture is very clear and vivid, even with settings turned down. I am quite impressed with the mini LED ability to deliver much deeper blacks in movies and games. It was super easy for me to set up. The legs (or feet) just slide right into their slots and click into place with no other hardware required to install them. I have mine connected to my fiber optic internet connection via cat 6 cable. The peripherals are connected via high speed HDMI cables. The built-in speakers have decent sound quality, better than I expected in my modest apartment. I may invest in a sound bar in the future for improved “surround” sound effects that take advantage of the Dolby Atmos audio. It powers on instantly and has ZERO lag time when operating, putting it MILES ahead of any fire tv set I’ve owned before it. I became tired of the 3-year shelf life of my old Insignia, as the back light quit suddenly. I was willing to invest in a better quality built Sony television that should last for many years longer, instead of throwing away a cheap television every few years, since electronic waste is fast becoming a major problem today. I’ve had great success with Sony TVs in the past, including my first 40 inch Bravia HD TV I bought back in 2005, which still works great today as a second tv in my bedroom. title: Beautiful OLED picture and more capable than I expected

I was also impressed that at least one popular 3D game could be installed directly on the TV as an app, with no console or PC. I connected my Bluetooth controller and played it directly on the TV. I wasn't expecting that. It looked like it was running at fairly minimal graphics quality, but it was playing and my controller worked.

This TV is very thin, and the instructions warn not to pinch the screen with your thumb when lifting it. I can see why. The back has a thicker section, but the screen becomes extremely thin at the edges, so I handled it carefully.

The picture and color quality look excellent even from a very side-angle view, and the sound quality is excellent too.

It comes with two small but sturdy legs that screw onto the bottom. With the legs installed, it feels stable.

Power use has also been pretty low in my setup. My backup battery reports about 40W-90W depending on how bright the picture is. A dark movie can hover around 40W, while a mostly white screen can approach 100W. Most movies I've watched hover around 60W, considerably less than my old TV used.

The remote is quite nice. I turned on Gemini mode in the TV settings, and I can press and hold the microphone button on the remote and speak naturally to it. It hears me clearly from across the room, and I can use my voice to run searches.

title: Ok, I get it. I now understand the OLED hype
body:
Our old 1080 TV in the master bedroom was in dire need of replacing. One of my friends had mentioned many times that switching to OLEDs made movie watching so much more immersive and special. I always kind of brushed it off over the top hyperbole.

I got this in and set up in the bedroom. Setup was dead simple. I just swapped over the cabling to our sound bar and network from our old TV into this and everything just worked. There was a quick initial firmware update that I let complete before starting to watch something. I was too anxious to see the picture quality and skipped over the calibration. I need to go back and do that still.

The initial images were as good as my friend had been telling me. When you hear "truly black blacks" you don't really comprehend it until you see it in person. The dark areas of the screen are a black hole of zero light. There is no bleed. The colors are bright and sharp against the deep inky blacks. We watched Project Hail Mary in 4K HDR IMAX and the spacewalk scenes were mind-blowing and sharp as a tack. We watched an F1 race this morning and the colors were vibrant and the crowds were made up of actual people instead of vaguely people-shaped objects.

I can't comment on the built-in GoogleTV bits as I just plugged my own Google Streamer and am using that exclusively for now. Same for the audio quality as we are using an external sound bar connected through the optical port.

What I realized very quickly was that this TV was going to cost me a lot of money. It'll do that by making me NEED to upgrade the 80" TV in our living room now. After watching movies on this 55" OLED I really don't want to go back to our old LED Sony TV. Pictures of a TV screen do the actual image no justice at all. You really just have to see it for yourself.

title: Stunning
body:
The Bravia 8 was a replacement for a 16-year-old Sharp 52-inch, which abruptly perished on night. With that large leap in technology, the improvement in visuals was breathtaking. Sony's build quality is impressive as well. This was a great purchase.

However... I do have a few general industry-wide caveats, which are the reason I can't honestly give my Bravia 8 the full 5 stars it would otherwise easily qualify for.

* The Bravia 8 doesn't get along with the rest of my system as well as the ancient Sharp it replaced. I'm sure this isn't a Sony thing, nor a Bravia 8 thing. It's the move toward ever-'smarter' components - each of which wants to run things it's own way. Going through the inevitable 'control my other devices' setup only makes the conflicts worse - I wish there was a setting to tell all the devices to just mind their own business. I'd still be using four remotes, but at least I wouldn't have my control inputs being constantly over-ridden.

* Along with the uppity built-in smarts, there's a serious dearth of available technical over-rides and read-outs. For instance, I've got a PC hooked up, and it's hit or miss whether the TV will recognize the correct resolution - and there's no manual setting to brute-force the resolution. At the same time, while my cable (IPTV) box is delivering a superb image, there's no way to confirm that it and the TV are in fact doing the promised 4K, or just getting by on really good 1080p - and, again, no easy way to enforce that outcome.

* The TV really wants individual HDMI devices to be plugged directly into it. And yet, after a full agonizing day, I was unable to get Audio Return Channel working - either via HDMI or optical connection - to provide full surround sound through my receiver. So I wasted another sweaty hour putting things back the way they were in the first place - everything plugged into the receiver, with a single HDMI connection to the TV. That setup is still quirky and mysterious (as much the fault of the receiver as the TV), but nonetheless, things feel a lot more rational this way.

* On the positive side, the TV has not been overbearing about Internet connectivity. I get an occasional warning popup to the effect that my Ethernet cable is disconnected, and so far that's it. On the negative side, I did need to enable GoogleTV at least once for the purposes of configuration (see next point). But back on the positive side, GoogleTV is quite functional, and obviously benefits from Google's extensive Android experience. If my TV simply *must* have an OS, I guess it's just as well to have a good one.

* In order to properly set up the picture, I needed to run a professional calibration app in GoogleTV - this instantly enabled a full range of picture settings in the Bravia on-screen menus. Having worked in computers and consumer electronics for decades, I do not enjoy being 'protected' from using my lifetime of know-how. The full settings could be disabled by default, yet made safely accessible behind a simple warning message.

* Accessing the full settings is important, because even in Professional mode I found the image drastically over-saturated. Once I'd turned the saturation down (and boosted the gamma very slightly to compensate for the fact that I run at low brightness), the image became astonishingly life-like. Watching talk-shows and the like, I often feel that the presenters are in the room with me.

Bottom line: Bravia 8 - full marks, it's a terrific TV. The OLED blacks are miraculous, the color gamut is gorgeous, and even older DVD-quality content looks better than ever before. Consumer industry: continuing failing grade, you need to wise up a bit!

Both loaded seamlessly after username/pw verification. Next I cycled through the Settings options several times to check and/or change/re-check the settings. I’d really recommend familiarizing yourself with all the settings and googling separately on your phone if you’re unsure what a particular setting does. Today I connected the DVD player via HDMI, turned on the Sony, and expected it to notice that a DVD player was connected, just as a computer would do. That didn’t happen. In fact after connecting the DVD successfully I spent HOURS trying to get the picture to display on the Sony screen. Jumped through so many hoops that I don’t recall how I fixed it. Let’s just say that it works now. But what a battle. Other observations: The sound is…ok. A sound bar would be a good addition. Picture: Great! Remote: Just stupid. I taped over Netflix and the other buttons to streaming services that don’t interest me. (Sony must’ve been gifted a tidy sum to include these companies on their remote.) Overall: I’d recommend this purchase if you can be patient and try various settings (if needed) through trial and error. This is a very nice tv.

body: Day 1-item arrived early in the day, unboxing and set up were pretty straight forward. I am very happy with the display of this television. Okay-so a mere 48 hours after receiving and setting up the TV, the ARC/eARC function on the TV stopped working! Just for no reason at all-it wasn't working, and it was impossible to reprogram ARC/eARC to work again. Wading through hell and high water, I just unplugged all the HDMI cables from the TV and my receiver. Unplugged the TV and the receiver. LEt them both sit for about 10 minutes. Reconnected everything and still did a hard reset on the TV and finally-i was able to assign HDMI ports and get sound to my receiver again! I hope I won't have to deduct another star. I really want to like this TV! Day 9-back to a 5 star rating. The Arc/eArc function on TV has been working properly for the past 7 days. I guess everything has settled in and TV has been everything I hoped it would be. I am pleased with this purchase. Update again-2 weeks later and the Arc/eArc feature is back to not working properly. it turns off my AV receiver, but it won't turn it on! I am keeping this at a 4 star. Very disappointing. Update June 2025- 4 months, 3 software updates, 1 remote control software update later and this TV is FINALLY operating correctly on a regular basis for the past 9 days. I put it back to a 5 star rating-but will keep my fingers crossed! Update 6/26 After owning this TV for a little over a year-it is substandard! The Arc/eARC works when it wants to and the CEC feature from my AV receiver is no longer recognized by the TV. So those features just stopped working! OLED definitely has the edge in pure picture quality, but this Mini LED still looks very good once properly tuned.

After 6 days of use and some tweaking to the picture and sound settings for my room, I’m really happy with it. For more than half the price of an OLED, it delivers solid performance. The bonus of 5 free movie credits and 100 free movies on the Sony Core app is a nice extra.

Great TV, fast delivery, and excellent packaging. I’m satisfied with my purchase and would recommend it.

title: Fantastic Quality Sony television with incredible 4K upscaling at a reasonable price
body: This TV is well worth the money with fantastic picture quality using my PS5, my Apple TV 4K, and the built-in google OS. The Dolby Vision HDR is impressive. The picture is very clear and vivid, even with settings turned down. I am quite impressed with the mini LED ability to deliver much deeper blacks in movies and games. It was super easy for me to set up. The legs (or feet) just slide right into their slots and click into place with no other hardware required to install them. I have mine connected to my fiber optic internet connection via cat 6 cable. The peripherals are connected via high speed HDMI cables. The built-in speakers have decent sound quality, better than I expected in my modest apartment. I may invest in a sound bar in the future for improved “surround” sound effects that take advantage of the Dolby Atmos audio. It powers on instantly and has ZERO lag time when operating, putting it MILES ahead of any fire tv set I’ve owned before it. I became tired of the 3-year shelf life of my old Insignia, as the back light quit suddenly. I was willing to invest in a better quality built Sony television that should last for many years longer, instead of throwing away a cheap television every few years, since electronic waste is fast becoming a major problem today. I’ve had great success with Sony TVs in the past, including my first 40 inch Bravia HD TV I bought back in 2005, which still works great today as a second tv in my bedroom. My only complaint is that only two of the four HDMI plugs are 2.1. You really do get what you pay for!

title: This is a great tv.
body:
I ordered this TV after both my 77” OLEDs failed — my LG lasted only 3 years, and my Samsung barely made it 3 months. I’m done with OLED technology; it just doesn’t hold up.

I decided to switch to this 75” Sony Mini LED, and I’m glad I did. I’ve owned Sony TVs before and they’ve always been reliable. The picture quality took a bit of adjustment at first — OLED and LED are very different. OLED definitely has the edge in pure picture quality, but this Mini LED still looks very good once properly tuned.

After 6 days of use and some tweaking to the picture and sound settings for my room, I’m really happy with it. For more than half the price of an OLED, it delivers solid performance. The bonus of 5 free movie credits and 100 free movies on the Sony Core app is a nice extra.

Great TV, fast delivery, and excellent packaging. I’m satisfied with my purchase and would recommend it.

title: Fantastic Quality Sony television with incredible 4K upscaling at a reasonable price
body: This TV is well worth the money with fantastic picture quality using my PS5, my Apple TV 4K, and the built-in google OS. The Dolby Vision HDR is impressive. The picture is very clear and vivid, even with settings turned down. I am quite impressed with the mini LED ability to deliver much deeper blacks in movies and games. It was super easy for me to set up. The legs (or feet) just slide right into their slots and click into place with no other hardware required to install them. I have mine connected to my fiber optic internet connection via cat 6 cable. The peripherals are connected via high speed HDMI cables. The built-in speakers have decent sound quality, better than I expected in my modest apartment. I may invest in a sound bar in the future for improved “surround” sound effects that take advantage of the Dolby Atmos audio. It powers on instantly and has ZERO lag time when operating, putting it MILES ahead of any fire tv set I’ve owned before it. I became tired of the 3-year shelf life of my old Insignia, as the back light quit suddenly. I was willing to invest in a better quality built Sony television that should last for many years longer, instead of throwing away a cheap television every few years, since electronic waste is fast becoming a major problem today. I’ve had great success with Sony TVs in the past, including my first 40 inch Bravia HD TV I bought back in 2005, which still works great today as a second tv in my bedroom. My only complaint is that only two of the four HDMI plugs are 2.1. You really do get what you pay for!

title: This does not come with a tv mount included. Purchase one separately. Vesa Universal TV mount
body:
I had my Roku set up for my older tv. Tv finally died on me, so this one was pretty much plug and play. Including using my old Vespa Universal TV mount. Sound bar and everything immediately synced in. With that being said I just had to tweak new settings to kids, so my child doesn't have problems from the TV being too bright.

The package came in another box layered on top of the store-bought box. Inside the box is a layer of thick Styrofoam and hard air cushioned plastic corners with an easy to life off box as the bottom is already open somewhat. So, this TV opens somewhat like a matchbox, be mindful you may want help as you don't want the tv to fall over. I learned the hard way upon opening that the TV did not have an included TV stand. Lucky for me, my old dead TV had a universal TV mount. Easy unscrew and screw on due to my old TV mount being a universal mount for certain sizes.

The visual on this TV after I set it up to just scan and some random option to play settings to bypass color and brightness to a universal setting was marvelous. The Netflix series the Witcher preview was one of the first things I saw, which was a lot of black mixed in with lightning. It is very hard to see a black monster, in black water in a black background, but I was able to see every feature with astounding clarity. That being said this TV made older sourced movies and shows seem somewhat 3d rendered as the images that focus up front stood out more as if getting that mirage feel from a portrait.

I have been playing games for more than two decades and sitting in front of a 4k monitor so looking at a lesser quality tv due to certain DPI modes and settings stands out to me. That being said, issues of blooming does appear on this TV but it is so rare and infrequent that you may not even notice unless someone points it out to you or you specifically look for it. In Dr. Sleep, there is a brief image of light going through a window, the blooming occurred on the edge of a window ledge that stood out too uniformed. Which in all fairness you can see this on an IPHONE 16 pro picture on some people's hairs. So, the best way to say this, is that if you like your high-quality images on an IPHONE 16 or similar camera pixel, this is what you are looking at for your TV shows for this quality of TV. I am still astounded that this TV literally makes images look somewhat 3d without glasses.

I have seen the LG C5 version in Cosco. I cannot vouch the same crisp image as I can for my iPhone on the C5. But do keep in mind source images matter and I don't think some people realize they should see the TV at the start of when it got turned on and 12 hours later running constantly. You may be surprised that some TVs will begin to stutter. Which may ruin your TV binging.

Gotta love the thin bezel. Almost see pure screen like the old Plasma days. That being said, I believe this is akin to a Plasma TV, except much lighter in weight.

Notes.

TV Vesa table mounting was easy.

I am using and have been using 8k HDMI cables. Which is good for multiple things but mainly for sound and video quality as my TV is connected to a LG soundbar which pretty much connects plug and play on this tv. Look for a deal on 8K and set it and forget it to get maximum quality and possibly zero chance of data stuttering.

A 55 to a 65 inch gains a reported 40 percent more tv volume space.

Be mindful of seller's choice of vendor as Fed Ex did not call to set up an appointment for me.

You will need to have a Vesa universal tv mount ready for this if you decide to put the tv on a table as it only comes with the wall mount attachment.

title: Gorgeous display.
body: Pros: * Brightness. Pushes 2000+ nits in HDR. It's wild how bright it can get. * Colors. I upgraded from an LG CX and I'm seeing shades of color I've never seen before. * Refresh rate. 165hz on PC is super smooth. * Very low input latency. This TV's very fast in game mode. * Crazy fast pixel response times. * Metal frame makes it easier to handle and move around than the CX was. * Cable management channel on the back keeps things super clean. Cons: * The remote lacks a set of buttons for switching inputs directly. Having to push the menu key and hold it to change inputs feels clunky. I may end up getting a new remote so I don't have to deal with that. * You have to enable 165hz mode. It's not a big deal but it's tucked in the menu in a way that wasn't very intuitive to find. I thought I needed a new HDMI cable until I found it. It's located in Settings > General > Game Optimizer, which you have to enable to turn on 165hz mode. It's great once it's on, though. * Gamma flicker when there's a significant fluctuation in frame rate while gaming on PC. It's only noticeable when there's a big drop but it's hard to miss when that happens. Frame gen helps smooth that out but shader compilation can cause an occasional flash. Inherent problem with gaming on OLED. * The fast pixel response times make it really hard to avoid judder in panning shots on low frame rate content. Some movies handle it fine, others can look like a slide show. I'm still tweaking the de-judder setting to see if I can find a balance I'm happy with. Inherent problem with OLED caused by the crazy fast pixel response times. I tested several very dark games, including Cronos, Dead Space remake, and Death Stranding 2 at night to see if I could spot any dithering. I can't. Image looks pristine aside from the listed issues, which are all inherent problems with OLED.

title: Fabulous Picture But Some Quirks, Too
body: Our 17-year old Panasonic plasma TV was starting to get 'glitchy' and I didn't want anything drastic to happen during the World Series - all of the reviews for the G5 LG OLED TVs were very convincing and I couldn't agree more but with a couple of exceptions. I worked with LG tech support and they said they were going to send someone out but that never happened - many online reviews complained of the same thing. I can compensate by cranking up the volume on the Marantz but something's wrong. I went so far as to request a return for the TV from Amazon but changed my mind and decided to keep the TV, its low volume notwithstanding. The volume level from the TV's internal speakers was fine but they don't compare to my stereo system. Through all the research I did, it never became clear that the TV comes with a wall mount bracket. It was simple enough to install although the printed instructions were terrible but the video on LG's website made it much easier. Speaking of printed instructions, the TV comes with none and the online user's manual is a complete joke - it mostly covers how to connect peripheral devices using hexadecimal code. There are on-screen instructions but they're very weak. Call me old fashioned but I prefer a complete, detailed printed manual. Also, there are very few connection ports on the back of the TV - I can no longer watch DVDs from my ancient Sony carousel DVD player as the TV has no component video input ports. Progress, I guess. I love the way the TV sits so close to the wall and I thought I would like the Gallery+ feature but I don't. Regardless, I enjoy the TV and I'm pleased with my decision to keep it.

title: Why I chose the LG G5. It wasn’t easy!
body: The choice was between the Samsung S95F, Sony Bravia 8 II and the LG G5. All very similar. I had read and watched all mainstream reviews and comparisons. Absorbed the technical nuances of QD-OLED v Tandem OLED, etc. My reality: I needed it to sit on a console exactly the width of a 65” TV. I have glass patio doors directly behind my sofa. It would be fed by an Apple TV with audio fed into a high end stereo system. So TV OS and sound were for me immaterial. Sony: generally rated the best image for film content but not so good for reflected ambient light. Excellent sound which I wouldn’t use. But….insane design of legs positioned at the very edges of the TV and extending slightly further. Ugly to my eye but more importantly wouldn’t fit on my console. (I have an 11 year old Bravia with very similar design but two positions to attach the feet: edge and mid way to center). Samsung: terrific design and the remote electronics is brilliant. Seemed the obvious choice for my ambient lighting situation but in bright light the matt screen has elevated black level and for me: no Dolby Vision is an absolute deal breaker. Sorry Samsung! LG: I have had an LG OLED for the past 7 years and it has performed flawlessly. Brand loyalty. Very bright but less reflected light rejection according to the reviews. But if Sony is killing sales due to feet positioning, LG is surely slaughtering sales by not including a stand and the stand (for the 55” and 65”) in turn being generally totally unavailable currently. I somehow managed to secure a 55” stand on B&H. The stand itself is the same for both. I can understand only wall mount do 77” or larger but 55”, 65”? The LG 5 year warranty is certainly a plus. But LG has a reputation for product reliability, more so than Samsung evidently. Cosmetically, the set has some (frame) depth as it was designed to sit flush on the wall. I personally love the ‘paper’ thin screen edge on my old LG and on the Samsung, but you won’t see it while watching. My experience: firstly set up: Filmmaker Mode on the G5 as everyone recommends. But key is to set the Apple TV > Video & Audio > 4K SDR (not 4K HDR or Dolby Vision) and Match Content Range & Frame Rate. This is absolutely critical. Otherwise SDR content, eg cable TV will look very dim. If the content is HDR/Dolby Vision, the Apple TV will automatically switch. And once set, my experience for most content: window reflection during the day virtually disappears. Yes, the reviews suggest otherwise, but real world it is fine and the contrast is evidently higher than the Samsung. And about the G5 stand: it turns out the stand is indeed the same, but the package also includes a plastic cover to cosmetically cover up where the included wall bracket would go if wall mounted and a second to cover up the cabling. And that second cover is a different size for the 55” and 65” which is why they have different SKUs! I’m hoping to find someone who bought the 65” stand for the 55” out of desperation so I can swap covers but you’d only see the absence of the cosmetic cover if you looked at the back of the TV. The G5 is fabulous, but you would probably not notice much of a difference between these three top rated TV’s even if you had them side by side. Maybe not Sony during the day with my room layout. Certainly Sony designers and LG marketers have worked hard to undermine their respective product sales and, from my point of view, Samsung too as the only major manufacturer on the market to refuse to license Dolby Vision in which most of my extensive collection of Apple TV movies are encoded. Maybe I wouldn’t notice the HDR+ rendition but I can’t believe the license fee saving hasn’t impacted sales revenues more. I hope some prospective buyers find this useful.
