title: 2026 Review - PC 165Hz Gaming Setup
body: OK PC gamers - you're probably getting sick of reviews talking about how pretty the picture is? (No question - the LG G5 is superior in picture quality when compared to standard Q-LED, and bright as h.ll). But I want to assure you that you can achieve 165Hz on your "modern" PC at 4K resolution, and definitely by using a certified HDMI 2.1 (a.k.a. Ultra HD) cable. For starters, I'm using an RTX 4080 video card, which I connected using a fiber optic 4K cable (from Amazon type in: 8K Fiber Optic HDMI Cable 6 FT) - should be around $30 USD. No, you do not need a fiber optic cable - but, you just purchased a premium/flagship TV - so why skimp on cable quality? Search Internet for compatible GPU's that have the HDMI 2.1 standard (if necessary). Setup Challenges: > Update the firmware to the LG G5 (current software version 33.22.65 as of 1/1/2026). This current version is stable, and you can go to the LG website and download software to a thumb drive if you want this particular version. Otherwise, let the TV do the update. Note: I personally turn off auto-updates to avoid unnecessary crashes caused by polluted updates. > Update your AMD or NVIDIA drivers to at least a 2025 version (depending on what GPU you own). I downloaded the latest driver (591.59 of December 18, 2025) from Nvidia's website for RTX(Geforce). The focus of the latest updates is that Nvidia is recognizing the HDMI 2.1 standard and Win11 tuning. > Once you have driver/firmware happiness, you must set up the port between your PC and TV; > Connect cable(s) and turn on PC, then select the port on the LG G5 (in my case it's HDMI port #1, which is usually the most capable port on any TV) > You must fully setup the LG TV first; go to Settings >>> General >>> scroll down to Game Optimizer (which has 15 different sub-settings) > In Game Optimizer you should see selection for; [165Hz Mode], [VRR & G-Sync], and [FreeSync Premium]. Of course I turned on 165Hz Mode and VRR & G-Sync because I have an RTX4080. I do not need FreeSync because the LG G5 is Nvidia "G-Sync Ready". > In the NVidia control panel (and I recommend searching the Internet for additional settings), you should be able to navigate to the Resolution tab and see that the LG G5 is reporting "3840 x 2160 (4K UHD) - Native, with a refresh rate of 165Hz" under the PC heading. Warning: if you are not familiar with changing NVidia settings, please refer to the Internet for guidance and morale support. Of course, you will want to fine tune the rest of your Nvidia and Windows settings to MAXimum Performance to achieve Greatness. I hope this helps...

title: Defective after 7 months - LG giving us the runaround
body: Bought tv in late Nov. It arrived in early Dec. Had professionals mount on wall. TV worked fine for 7 months. Then in July, picture went dark and we noticed something like burn marks along the bottom right edge. 15 burn marks in total, all similar size and equidistant apart. Immediately called LG customer service and they tried to say we damaged the tv, even after we told them the tv was mounted 7 months earlier and not physically touched since. We also mentioned that we had the same tv in a smaller size, which was also mounted and had no problems with the tv. LG held firm and said we damaged the tv so it was not covered under warranty. We continued to insist it was a manufacturer's defect so LG finally said a repair technician would have to look at the tv and determine how the damage was caused. They told me to call a repair and gave me the names of three repair shops. The nearest shop was 1.5 hours away and the farthest was 2.5 hours away in another state. Needless to say, we do not live in their service areas. LG finally said they would find a repair tech and estimated 7-10 days to set up the appointment. Every few days, LG would send a text message saying it was taking longer than expected but my request remains a priority. Finally, after more than two weeks, LG requested I send the proof of purchase and the serial sticker on the back of the tv. I sent both same day and asked LG to acknowledge receipt and inform of next steps... no reply. Two days later, I asked for acknowledgement again... no reply. Two days later, LG sent a text saying they tried to get a hold of me but I did not reply so they were closing the case. I immediately called customer service. The rep sent the same request for PoP and serial sticker from a different phone number. I sent both while on the phone and she confirmed receipt. She said she would put me on hold while adding the documents to my case and ensuring it was reopened. While on hold, the connection was lost and I received a text message from LG saying "Will confirm once documents attached - send you text later." ------ Obviously, we are extremely frustrated. We have asked to speak to Supervisors multiple times, but LG always refuses. We have asked for a refund or a new tv, but LG says they can't confirm the damage was a manufacturers defect. This has been dragging on for nearly a month and there is no end in sight. I can only conclude that LG is trying to find ways to get out of honoring their warranty. Will never buy from LG again.

title: Amazing picture quality. I hate the OS
body:
TL;DR

Amazing picture quality with different picture modes for different types of content and lighting conditions. Impressive sound quality for a TV. Annoying OS and Home Screen.

In depth review and initial thoughts:

This tv is a HUGE improvement over my previous one- which was a Samsung UN55C5000 from 2010.. that being said my old tv was still in great shape and still had an acceptable image quality- so even though this new tv is definitely on the pricey side I have confidence that it should last me quite some time.

Even though I have been daily driving a 16 year old tv, over the years I have seen my fair share of televisions. 4k smart TVs are kind of a dime a dozen these days- you can buy them for a couple hundred dollars at pretty much any retailer - but that doesn’t mean they are all created equal. Many have left me less than impressed with the image quality, and the “smart features” were usually clunky. I didn’t want to spend a couple hundred dollars for a small “upgrade” that would probably need to be replaced in a couple years. I wanted something that made me fall in love with tv and watching films again.

And that’s where this Samsung 65” QN80H comes in.

From the first time turning it on I was captivated by then colours, brightness and clarity. I will admit, I do hate how you need to set up and make accounts for everything these days. It’s super annoying, it takes like half an hour to get everything sorted: making a new Samsung account only to find out I already have an account for some super old phone or device from who knows when. I of course can’t remember the password, so I’m making a new account or doing the password recovery thing… tedious. Luckily, the Tv is super responsive to input commands from the menu. Everything feels very snappy. I’ve used cheaper TVs and trying to navigate anything is super slow and sluggish- that is absolutely not the case here, so that took some of the pain away from the set up.

Then of course I need to sign into all my streaming accounts- which isn’t too bad, and just something you need to do with new devices regardless so no point complaining there. Again, the responsiveness made it not as bad. What was bad though was just trying to navigate the OS in general and the App Store in particular. That experience was frustrating. I had to scroll through WAY TOO MANY apps to find the ones I wanted. The search would only search for content. Then you finally find the app you want, install it and “add it to Home Screen” so it takes you back to the Home Screen, then you need to go back to the app selection and scroll through everything AGAIN. Super super annoying.

Now that I’ve got my main apps downloaded and signed in, I can actually start exploring the TV. I have a few more annoyances before I get into the good… but I promise despite all these annoyances I do really like this- it’s just unfortunate that these initial interactions are the first things I have to deal with.

The main OS screen shows you all kinds of shows- from some from streaming services you have, but mostly from ones I don’t. What’s worse is that it will show me movies or shows that ARE on a service I have (in this case Crave) but it doesn’t tell me it’s on crave, instead tells me I can rent or buy it on Amazon Prime or Apple TV. I don’t think you can change this either. Ideally your Home Screen would ONLY show you things from services you have installed/ are logged in to so that you could seamlessly just use your tv to browse all the content from across all the services you have. Instead it just makes the main page frustrating and useless, and I still need to resort to third party apps on my phone when searching for specific shows and trying to find if they’re on a service i have already. Right now the Home Screen is basically a store front/ advertisement, which I personally dislike… a lot.

While we’re still on the topic of the menu: it does have a bunch of different features at the top- live channels, music, to connect Spotify, gaming, art, and apps.

Live channels has a bunch of live stuff from the Samsung plus. It’s mostly just easy to watch mindless reality-esque stuff on “channels” that play different episodes of the same show over and over. Not for everyone, but sometimes some nice trash! I believe it also features local new channels which is actually nice.

The Spotify stuff is self explanatory: connect your Spotify account and listen to music. I definitely wouldn’t be buying this tv just to listen to music, but it’s a nice option to have built in and the sound quality is actually pretty good!

Gaming has both integrated free basic games you can play with your remote to cloud based streaming things via stuff like Xbox and GeForce, which is kind of cool. I only have played some of the free built in games like Tetris and word jumble game but it was interesting. My wife and I played one of the games for like 2 hours and lost track of time. Very cool! I probably won’t use the cloud gaming stuff as I have a pretty beefy pc I play on myself already, and I sure don’t need ANOTHER subscription or account to pay for and keep track of.

The art I guess is art work you can display on your tv when not in use. Samsung make the “frame” tv, so this makes lots of sense for that. I don’t mount my tv on my wall because I don’t like looking up at my tv when I’m watching it. I guess if you’re one of those people and don’t want a big black rectangle on the wall when the tv isn’t in use then this would be handy. Personally, I don’t care about it.

We’ve already touched on the apps. One more thing to mention is there’s just SO MANY… scrolling at full speed (which is fast) takes over 10 seconds to get through the whole list. The fact that I can’t easily search that list is nuts.

Now that we’ve explored the TV, let’s talk about the picture quality: it’s fantastic. It’s so bright, and the colours are so vibrant. The blacks are pretty black (not quite OLED levels, but definitely nothing you’ll really notice without pixel peeping). It has a handful of different picture modes that you can change between depending on the content and when/ where you’re viewing it. Some stuff I like to watch on dynamic, other I used the Filmmaker mode. I found during the day with bright windows I liked the dynamic setting even for movies, while at night the same movie was too bright and punchy but looked amazing on filmmaker mode- while during the day the filmmaker mode was too dim.

The picture is super crisp and sharp. The viewing angle is best from head on- but it’s definitely more than acceptably viewable at any angle you’d reasonably be watching this from. I don’t game on this- but if I did, the higher refresh rate would be an appreciated feature for devices that allowed it.

The auto adjustment features are actually kind of nice, to adjust different lighting conditions and time of day so you’re not having to constantly be doing it yourself.

The audio quality as I already touched on is great for a tv. It sounds full yet everything can be clearly heard. I’m not an audiophile and a little hard of hearing so I can’t really comment on the nuances - but it carry’s through a room pretty well, and provides more than acceptable quality out of the box for regular viewing, though I’m sure lots of people will opt for external audio speakers and solutions for that real cinematic experience.

I personally hate the clear motion, or whatever the motion smoothing is called on this TV. I hate it on all TVs and turn it off immediately. It might be good for sports- I don’t really watch sports though so I’m not sure. While we’re on the subject of turning things off— do yourself a favour a poke around the privacy controls. There’s some settings you will definitely want to disable. Google them for the latest names and what they essentially do- but the big one (which is on most smart TVs) is the one that essentially takes screenshots of your screen every few seconds and breaks it down for ai to analyze it so that you can get oddly specific ads based on everything you do on your tv, whether is via streaming or not. Big brother is watching. Disable that. Every smart device or anything connected to the internet is basically spying on you. It probably still will be in some way, but learn about and be aware of what your devices are tracking.

Overall, I am very happy with this tv, despite most my review being complaining about things. A lot of people seem to be frustrated with the OS stuff as well and get a third party solution like an Apple TV or Firestick, which I understand but also think it kind of defeats the purpose of a smart TV. I don’t know how it compares to most other smart TV OS’s, but because of the OS I am removing one star. I wish I could remove 1.25 or so, since I think this issue is worth more than a 1 star reduction but not worth 2. Without these OS issues this would easily be a 5 star TV worth the money.

title: Very Impressive Quality, but Also a Quite Expensive Mini LED TV
body:
The Samsung QN80H is a very impressive Mini LED TV thanks to its high brightness, and premium looking picture quality. The Quantum Mini LED panel gives the image a very clean and refined look, especially with higher quality content like 4K HDR10+ movies, and games. During darker settings, like the evening or when you can limit the natural light in the room, the picture can get surprisingly close to OLED quality, with good contrast and depth. I found the Filmmaker Mode to be the best-looking and most detailed picture option when the room is not too bright, but during the day I sometimes have to switch to Standard or other brighter modes because it can look a bit dim when there's too much natural light (especially when watching content with darker scenes). I would avoid using the AI Auto modes for picture, as they tend to make the picture look washed out and worsens the overall quality of the content you're watching.

Compared to some of last year's OLEDs, like the Samsung S90F and LG C5 OLED TVs, the QN80H holds up better than I expected, but the OLEDs still have the edge overall. The QN80H gets very bright, handles daytime viewing well, and does not have the same long-term burn-in concerns that some people still worry about with OLEDs. This makes it a better option for brighter rooms, but you will still need to adjust the picture during the day if you have large windows that bring in a natural light. However, OLEDs still have better black levels, more precise contrast, and that extra depth since each pixel can turn off individually (which can't for this TV). Since the QN80H is under $1800 and the both of last year's OLED models are just barely more at closer to $2000, it's hard to justify the QN80H unless you are really worried about the potential burn-in with OLEDs often watch TV in bright environments, or find this TV on a better sale.

Compared to Samsung's lower end Mini LEDs, like the M80H and M70H, the QN80H is a better performing Mini LED option. The picture looks more refined than both the M70H and M80H, with better contrast, better overall depth, and a more premium look thanks to the Quantum Mini LED panel. That said, the M80H does get surprisingly close for nearly half the price, which this TV a worse value value than the M80H for most people. The M70H on the other hand is a much more budget version, with a worse picture, only a 60Hz panel, and a less premium experience overall. The QN80H is the better TV, but the M80H makes the price jump harder to justify.

Setup was mostly straightforward, but Samsung’s account and SmartThings process can slow things down if you don't already have an account. If you have a Samsung account ready and a Samsung device connected to the WiFi, setup can be around 5-10 minutes, but creating a new Samsung account without any connected devices seemed to make it take closer to 15-20 minutes. The built-in sound is pretty good for a flat-panel TV, but with a TV this nice I would still recommend at least external speakers, and ideally an AVR with larger speakers. I also like Samsung’s Tizen software overall, but wish it supported downloading popular VPN apps like you can on Google TV. That said, if you want to use a VPN you'll need to use one of the supported or look into using an external Google TV streaming box.

Overall, the QN80H is a really good TV with a great picture quality, strong brightness, fast performance, and great gaming support. It is also one of the best-performing Mini LED options from Samsung's 2026 line-up, but just make sure you appreciate the improvement over the M80H and want to take the jump to OLED.

Pros:

- Great picture quality with strong brightness, vibrant colours and sharp details.

- Quantum Mini LED gives the image a more premium look and gets surprisingly close to OLED quality in controlled lighting.

- 144Hz support, with a powerful processor is great for gaming.

- Built-in sound is pretty good for most average viewing.

- Great all-around TV for movies, sports, gaming, and streaming.

Cons:

- At under $1800, it is very close to OLED pricing without OLED performance, and quite a bit more than the more affordable M80H.

- AI display modes seem to make the picture look washed out.

- Filmmaker Mode looks great in controlled lighting, but can look dim with darker content during the day.

- Samsung account/SmartThings creation can really slow down the setup if not created ahead of time.

- Most popular VPN apps require an external Google TV box.

title: La télévision la plus impressionnante que j'aie eue, elle porte vraiment bien son nom
body:
La qualité d'image QLED est phénoménale, les couleurs sont vives et éclatantes, le noir est vraiment noir, le blanc vraiment blanc, et c'est aussi beau de près que de loin. Le 144 Hz se voit clairement, tout est fluide et les vidéos ne saccadent pas. La différence est réelle quand on vient d'une vieille TV 60 Hz.

Le traitement anti-reflet fonctionne incroyablement bien, car le soleil frappe directement sur ma TV et l'image reste tout aussi belle, aucune perte de visibilité ni de couleur. Je n'ai plus besoin de fermer les rideaux pour regarder la télévision. Et la barre de son intégrée, parlons-en!! Elle est impressionnante pour une TV aussi mince, mais genre vraiment. Le son Dolby est fort et immersif mais également personalisable avec l'égaliseur automatique et ou manuelle, personnellement entre 6 et 13/100 le volume est déjà suffisant, donc sa donne une idée de la puissance qu'elle a au maximum. Il est aussi possible de connecter des appareils Bluetooth comme des hauts-parleurs, système de son ou des écouteurs, bien que mes écouteurs RedMagic TWS Gaming soient détectés mais n'arrivent pas à s'y connecter pour une raison inconnue. Cependant, je suis quasi certain que les earbuds de Samsung et les AirPods de Apple serait compatible.

Côté intégration Samsung, il n'y a pas plus simple, la TV s'est connectée au WiFi toute seule via un code QR, et depuis mon cellulaire Samsung, je peux tout contrôler, changer de poste, ouvrir des applications, modifier le son et l'affichage, fermer ou ouvrir la TV, activer le mode art, faire du partage d'écran avec possibilité de le mettre en pause et de le reprendre sans tout relancer. En pratique, la télécommande devient presque optionnelle.

Pour le mode galerie, la bibliothèque d'œuvres d'art est payante, mais il est possible d'utiliser ses propres photos gratuitement et de les faire défiler. En zoomant avec la caméra du téléphone sur une œuvre affichée, on voit les coups de pinceau et les détails comme si c'était une vraie toile. C'est carrément bluffant. Le mode art est aussi optionnel : si on ne veut pas que la TV se transforme en cadre à la fermeture, il suffit de maintenir le bouton d'alimentation 3 secondes et la TV s'éteint complètement. Une fois que j'ai installé et configuré ma TV, j'ai envoyé une photo d'un oeuvre d'art à mon père, et il a cru pendant un court moment que c'était un très grand cadre photo. L'écran fait moins d'un pouce d'épaisseur, ce qui lui donne exactement l'apparence d'un tableau accroché au mur. Il faut se dire que moi, j'ai le contour de la TV qui est noir, mais cette TV a aussi l'option de contour en bois, ce qui rendrait sa encore plus difficile à savoir qu'il s'agît en réalité d'un TV et si on ajoute à sa qu'on passe le câble dans le mur, on vient de créer un nouveau jeu similaire au jeux "AI or not" : TV ou Cadre.

Je n'ai qu'un seul câble de branché pour que tout fonctionne, pas besoin d'un câble pour l'alimentation de la TV, d'un câble pour la barre de son etc, donc c'est très minimaliste.

Note : Le son et la qualité d'image dans la vidéo a mal été filmé par mon cellulaire car il n'est pas très récent, je vous assure que l'image ne n'est pas saturé comme ça (les photos prisent en sont la preuve) et que l'audio est 1000 fois meilleure que dans ma vidéo.

title: An Advanced Display Designed as Much for the Room as for the Viewer
body:
The Samsung Frame Pro is an advanced display designed as much for the room as for the viewer. Rather than simply producing another premium television, Samsung has clearly focused on creating a display that integrates into your living space without giving up the performance expected from a modern high-end TV.

Packaging was excellent, with everything needed for installation including the flush wall mount, tabletop feet, wireless hub, remote and accessories. The television itself is exceptionally thin and surprisingly heavy for its size, so I would strongly recommend two people for installation and lifting only by the frame edges.

The wireless hub is one of the standout features. HDMI devices, Ethernet, optical audio, antenna and USB storage all connect to the hub rather than directly to the television, allowing the display itself to remain almost cable-free with only a single visible power cable. It makes for an exceptionally clean installation and means adding or changing devices happens at the cabinet instead of behind a flush-mounted TV.

Initial setup took a little patience. Like many modern smart devices, the TV immediately performed a substantial firmware update. I encountered a few networking quirks during the very first setup (before updating), but once updated everything operated normally. This feels like the sort of one-time setup experience that many connected devices go through today rather than an ongoing issue.

The defining feature for me is the display itself. The anti-glare surface is unlike any television I’ve personally used. Instead of creating sharp, mirror-like reflections, overhead lights become soft, diffuse illumination that quickly disappears into the image once content is playing. Even more impressive is that Samsung accomplished this without noticeably softening the picture. Small text remained crisp, colours stayed accurate, and I found myself comfortably reading code and working from well off-center under bright room lighting.

Art Mode is what finally made the purpose of the Frame Pro click for me. Years ago, modern televisions reached the point where people walked into a showroom and said “wow” because of how impressive they looked while turned on. The Frame Pro gave me that same reaction while it was effectively “off.” Rather than looking like a large black rectangle hanging on the wall, it genuinely becomes part of the room. Samsung promotes its Art Store subscription, but you’re not locked into it, you can also load your own artwork or photos from USB storage.

Movie performance was equally impressive. I tested everything from high-contrast films like Sin City to modern, visually demanding movies with fast action and expansive scenery. The AI picture processing adapted well to different content, motion remained smooth, colours were rich without looking exaggerated, and the display was equally comfortable to watch in a bright daytime living room or a dark evening movie session.

Gaming exceeded my expectations as well. Connected to a PC, the display automatically negotiated 4K at 144 Hz, with higher refresh rates available at lower resolutions (although I did not specifically test 240 Hz operation). Detail, colour, responsiveness and smooth camera movement were all excellent, and the wireless hub introduced no noticeable lag or display issues while changing resolutions or switching between systems. The forgiving viewing angles and excellent anti-glare characteristics also make it a very comfortable display for casual couch gaming.

One use case that mattered to me was how naturally this television lends itself to becoming an “ephemeral workstation.” Pair the hub with a compact mini-PC or NUC tucked away in a cabinet, add a wireless keyboard and mouse or trackball, and the television becomes a clean, cable-free workstation when needed, then quietly returns to displaying artwork when you’re finished. The same concept works equally well for game streaming or a compact entertainment PC.

Sound quality is very nice for a TV alone, and would be perfectly fine without needing to be paired with a sound bar or external system, although they would offer enhanced sound experience.

This isn’t the television for someone who simply wants the biggest, brightest display that dominates the room. Samsung makes other models that lean more heavily in that direction. The Frame Pro takes a different approach. It impresses with subtlety. It delivers excellent performance for movies, television, gaming and even light workstation use while integrating into your living space in a way that no conventional television I’ve used has managed.

After spending time with it, I came away more impressed than I expected. It’s a premium display that successfully bridges high-performance entertainment with thoughtful interior design, and it accomplishes that goal remarkably well.

title: Impressive Art TV
body:
I was looking for a TV that would fit the aesthetic of my dining room, and this one is honestly beautiful. The installation process was straightforward using the included wall mount. Samsung includes a positioning guide in the box, which helped me align everything properly on the wall. One of the features I appreciate the most is the One Connect Box. Since it is separate from the TV, the only cable running to the screen is the power cable, which helps keep the setup looking very clean. I was able to place the One Connect Box inside a cabinet, making the installation even more discreet. After mounting the TV, I went through the setup process. It prompted me to use the SmartThings app on my phone, but unfortunately the setup failed twice. I ended up completing everything directly on the TV instead, and that worked without any issues.

Once the setup was finished, I pressed the power button on the remote and was immediately blown away by the Art Mode. I still cannot get over how realistic it looks. Unless I tell people it is a TV, most assume it is simply a large framed artwork hanging on the wall. That is really what makes this TV special. Art Mode automatically activates when you turn the TV off, and it works very well. There is an extensive built-in art gallery available through a subscription service, but you can also upload your own artwork and photos through the SmartThings app or by using a USB drive connected to the One Connect Box.

As for picture quality, it is excellent. The 4K image is incredibly sharp, and the QLED Mini LED panel with HDR delivers vibrant colors, impressive brightness, and excellent contrast. What is even more impressive is how matte the screen looks in Art Mode while still providing such a great picture quality when watching content. For gamers, the TV also supports up to 144Hz, although I did not test that feature since mine is installed in the dining room. Another nice feature is the anti-glare coating. Even with direct sunlight coming into the room, the screen remains easy to view. Watching darker movies during the day is not an issue at all.

The only aspect I do not particularly like is the software experience. The interface feels somewhat cluttered with features and recommendations I never use. Samsung TV Plus comes pre-installed and cannot be removed or hidden. There are also a lot of ads for renting or buying movie or shows that cannot be removed. The overall UI also feel a little bit slow and sluggish comparing to an Apple TV for example. That said, it can be worked around since you can simply connect a streaming device of your choice to the One Connect Box and bypass most of the built-in software experience. Doing so does not affect Art Mode in any way.

Overall, I think this is an excellent TV for anyone who wants the benefits of a modern television without compromising the look and aesthetic of their room.

author: James Best

title: Amazing picture quality. I hate the OS
body:
TL;DR

Amazing picture quality with different picture modes for different types of content and lighting conditions. Impressive sound quality for a TV. Annoying OS and Home Screen.

In depth review and initial thoughts:

This tv is a HUGE improvement over my previous one- which was a Samsung UN55C5000 from 2010.. that being said my old tv was still in great shape and still had an acceptable image quality- so even though this new tv is definitely on the pricey side I have confidence that it should last me quite some time.

Even though I have been daily driving a 16 year old tv, over the years I have seen my fair share of televisions. 4k smart TVs are kind of a dime a dozen these days- you can buy them for a couple hundred dollars at pretty much any retailer - but that doesn’t mean they are all created equal. Many have left me less than impressed with the image quality, and the “smart features” were usually clunky. I didn’t want to spend a couple hundred dollars for a small “upgrade” that would probably need to be replaced in a couple years. I wanted something that made me fall in love with tv and watching films again.

And that’s where this Samsung 65” QN80H comes in.

From the first time turning it on I was captivated by then colours, brightness and clarity. I will admit, I do hate how you need to set up and make accounts for everything these days. It’s super annoying, it takes like half an hour to get everything sorted: making a new Samsung account only to find out I already have an account for some super old phone or device from who knows when. I of course can’t remember the password, so I’m making a new account or doing the password recovery thing… tedious. Luckily, the Tv is super responsive to input commands from the menu. Everything feels very snappy. I’ve used cheaper TVs and trying to navigate anything is super slow and sluggish- that is absolutely not the case here, so that took some of the pain away from the set up.

Then of course I need to sign into all my streaming accounts- which isn’t too bad, and just something you need to do with new devices regardless so no point complaining there. Again, the responsiveness made it not as bad. What was bad though was just trying to navigate the OS in general and the App Store in particular. That experience was frustrating. I had to scroll through WAY TOO MANY apps to find the ones I wanted. The search would only search for content. Then you finally find the app you want, install it and “add it to Home Screen” so it takes you back to the Home Screen, then you need to go back to the app selection and scroll through everything AGAIN. Super super annoying.

Now that I’ve got my main apps downloaded and signed in, I can actually start exploring the TV. I have a few more annoyances before I get into the good… but I promise despite all these annoyances I do really like this- it’s just unfortunate that these initial interactions are the first things I have to deal with.

The main OS screen shows you all kinds of shows- from some from streaming services you have, but mostly from ones I don’t. What’s worse is that it will show me movies or shows that ARE on a service I have (in this case Crave) but it doesn’t tell me it’s on crave, instead tells me I can rent or buy it on Amazon Prime or Apple TV. I don’t think you can change this either. Ideally your Home Screen would ONLY show you things from services you have installed/ are logged in to so that you could seamlessly just use your tv to browse all the content from across all the services you have. Instead it just makes the main page frustrating and useless, and I still need to resort to third party apps on my phone when searching for specific shows and trying to find if they’re on a service i have already. Right now the Home Screen is basically a store front/ advertisement, which I personally dislike… a lot.

While we’re still on the topic of the menu: it does have a bunch of different features at the top- live channels, music, to connect Spotify, gaming, art, and apps.

Live channels has a bunch of live stuff from the Samsung plus. It’s mostly just easy to watch mindless reality-esque stuff on “channels” that play different episodes of the same show over and over. Not for everyone, but sometimes some nice trash! I believe it also features local new channels which is actually nice.

The Spotify stuff is self explanatory: connect your Spotify account and listen to music. I definitely wouldn’t be buying this tv just to listen to music, but it’s a nice option to have built in and the sound quality is actually pretty good!

Gaming has both integrated free basic games you can play with your remote to cloud based streaming things via stuff like Xbox and GeForce, which is kind of cool. I only have played some of the free built in games like Tetris and word jumble game but it was interesting. My wife and I played one of the games for like 2 hours and lost track of time. Very cool! I probably won’t use the cloud gaming stuff as I have a pretty beefy pc I play on myself already, and I sure don’t need ANOTHER subscription or account to pay for and keep track of.

The art I guess is art work you can display on your tv when not in use. Samsung make the “frame” tv, so this makes lots of sense for that. I don’t mount my tv on my wall because I don’t like looking up at my tv when I’m watching it. I guess if you’re one of those people and don’t want a big black rectangle on the wall when the tv isn’t in use then this would be handy. Personally, I don’t care about it.

We’ve already touched on the apps. One more thing to mention is there’s just SO MANY… scrolling at full speed (which is fast) takes over 10 seconds to get through the whole list. The fact that I can’t easily search that list is nuts.

Now that we’ve explored the TV, let’s talk about the picture quality: it’s fantastic. It’s so bright, and the colours are so vibrant. The blacks are pretty black (not quite OLED levels, but definitely nothing you’ll really notice without pixel peeping). It has a handful of different picture modes that you can change between depending on the content and when/ where you’re viewing it. Some stuff I like to watch on dynamic, other I used the Filmmaker mode. I found during the day with bright windows I liked the dynamic setting even for movies, while at night the same movie was too bright and punchy but looked amazing on filmmaker mode- while during the day the filmmaker mode was too dim.

The picture is super crisp and sharp. The viewing angle is best from head on- but it’s definitely more than acceptably viewable at any angle you’d reasonably be watching this from. I don’t game on this- but if I did, the higher refresh rate would be an appreciated feature for devices that allowed it.

The auto adjustment features are actually kind of nice, to adjust different lighting conditions and time of day so you’re not having to constantly be doing it yourself.

The audio quality as I already touched on is great for a tv. It sounds full yet everything can be clearly heard. I’m not an audiophile and a little hard of hearing so I can’t really comment on the nuances - but it carry’s through a room pretty well, and provides more than acceptable quality out of the box for regular viewing, though I’m sure lots of people will opt for external audio speakers and solutions for that real cinematic experience.

I personally hate the clear motion, or whatever the motion smoothing is called on this TV. I hate it on all TVs and turn it off immediately. It might be good for sports- I don’t really watch sports though so I’m not sure. While we’re on the subject of turning things off— do yourself a favour a poke around the privacy controls. There’s some settings you will definitely want to disable. Google them for the latest names and what they essentially do- but the big one (which is on most smart TVs) is the one that essentially takes screenshots of your screen every few seconds and breaks it down for ai to analyze it so that you can get oddly specific ads based on everything you do on your tv, whether is via streaming or not. Big brother is watching. Disable that. Every smart device or anything connected to the internet is basically spying on you. It probably still will be in some way, but learn about and be aware of what your devices are tracking.

Overall, I am very happy with this tv, despite most my review being complaining about things. A lot of people seem to be frustrated with the OS stuff as well and get a third party solution like an Apple TV or Firestick, which I understand but also think it kind of defeats the purpose of a smart TV. I don’t know how it compares to most other smart TV OS’s, but because of the OS I am removing one star. I wish I could remove 1.25 or so, since I think this issue is worth more than a 1 star reduction but not worth 2. Without these OS issues this would easily be a 5 star TV worth the money.

title: Very Impressive Quality, but Also a Quite Expensive Mini LED TV
body:
The Samsung QN80H is a very impressive Mini LED TV thanks to its high brightness, and premium looking picture quality. The Quantum Mini LED panel gives the image a very clean and refined look, especially with higher quality content like 4K HDR10+ movies, and games. During darker settings, like the evening or when you can limit the natural light in the room, the picture can get surprisingly close to OLED quality, with good contrast and depth. I found the Filmmaker Mode to be the best-looking and most detailed picture option when the room is not too bright, but during the day I sometimes have to switch to Standard or other brighter modes because it can look a bit dim when there's too much natural light (especially when watching content with darker scenes). I would avoid using the AI Auto modes for picture, as they tend to make the picture look washed out and worsens the overall quality of the content you're watching.

Compared to some of last year's OLEDs, like the Samsung S90F and LG C5 OLED TVs, the QN80H holds up better than I expected, but the OLEDs still have the edge overall. The QN80H gets very bright, handles daytime viewing well, and does not have the same long-term burn-in concerns that some people still worry about with OLEDs. This makes it a better option for brighter rooms, but you will still need to adjust the picture during the day if you have large windows that bring in a natural light. However, OLEDs still have better black levels, more precise contrast, and that extra depth since each pixel can turn off individually (which can't for this TV). Since the QN80H is under $1800 and the both of last year's OLED models are just barely more at closer to $2000, it's hard to justify the QN80H unless you are really worried about the potential burn-in with OLEDs often watch TV in bright environments, or find this TV on a better sale.

Compared to Samsung's lower end Mini LEDs, like the M80H and M70H, the QN80H is a better performing Mini LED option. The picture looks more refined than both the M70H and M80H, with better contrast, better overall depth, and a more premium look thanks to the Quantum Mini LED panel. That said, the M80H does get surprisingly close for nearly half the price, which this TV a worse value value than the M80H for most people. The M70H on the other hand is a much more budget version, with a worse picture, only a 60Hz panel, and a less premium experience overall. The QN80H is the better TV, but the M80H makes the price jump harder to justify.

Setup was mostly straightforward, but Samsung’s account and SmartThings process can slow things down if you don't already have an account. If you have a Samsung account ready and a Samsung device connected to the WiFi, setup can be around 5-10 minutes, but creating a new Samsung account without any connected devices seemed to make it take closer to 15-20 minutes. The built-in sound is pretty good for a flat-panel TV, but with a TV this nice I would still recommend at least external speakers, and ideally an AVR with larger speakers. I also like Samsung’s Tizen software overall, but wish it supported downloading popular VPN apps like you can on Google TV. That said, if you want to use a VPN you'll need to use one of the supported or look into using an external Google TV streaming box.

Overall, the QN80H is a really good TV with a great picture quality, strong brightness, fast performance, and great gaming support. It is also one of the best-performing Mini LED options from Samsung's 2026 line-up, but just make sure you appreciate the improvement over the M80H and want to take the jump to OLED.

Pros:

- Great picture quality with strong brightness, vibrant colours and sharp details.

- Quantum Mini LED gives the image a more premium look and gets surprisingly close to OLED quality in controlled lighting.

- 144Hz support, with a powerful processor is great for gaming.

- Built-in sound is pretty good for most average viewing.

- Great all-around TV for movies, sports, gaming, and streaming.

Cons:

- At under $1800, it is very close to OLED pricing without OLED performance, and quite a bit more than the more affordable M80H.

- AI display modes seem to make the picture look washed out.

- Filmmaker Mode looks great in controlled lighting, but can look dim with darker content during the day.

- Samsung account/SmartThings creation can really slow down the setup if not created ahead of time.

- Most popular VPN apps require an external Google TV box.

title: La télévision la plus impressionnante que j'aie eue, elle porte vraiment bien son nom
body:
La qualité d'image QLED est phénoménale, les couleurs sont vives et éclatantes, le noir est vraiment noir, le blanc vraiment blanc, et c'est aussi beau de près que de loin. Le 144 Hz se voit clairement, tout est fluide et les vidéos ne saccadent pas. La différence est réelle quand on vient d'une vieille TV 60 Hz.

Le traitement anti-reflet fonctionne incroyablement bien, car le soleil frappe directement sur ma TV et l'image reste tout aussi belle, aucune perte de visibilité ni de couleur. Je n'ai plus besoin de fermer les rideaux pour regarder la télévision. Et la barre de son intégrée, parlons-en!! Elle est impressionnante pour une TV aussi mince, mais genre vraiment. Le son Dolby est fort et immersif mais également personalisable avec l'égaliseur automatique et ou manuelle, personnellement entre 6 et 13/100 le volume est déjà suffisant, donc sa donne une idée de la puissance qu'elle a au maximum. Il est aussi possible de connecter des appareils Bluetooth comme des hauts-parleurs, système de son ou des écouteurs, bien que mes écouteurs RedMagic TWS Gaming soient détectés mais n'arrivent pas à s'y connecter pour une raison inconnue. Cependant, je suis quasi certain que les earbuds de Samsung et les AirPods de Apple serait compatible.

Côté intégration Samsung, il n'y a pas plus simple, la TV s'est connectée au WiFi toute seule via un code QR, et depuis mon cellulaire Samsung, je peux tout contrôler, changer de poste, ouvrir des applications, modifier le son et l'affichage, fermer ou ouvrir la TV, activer le mode art, faire du partage d'écran avec possibilité de le mettre en pause et de le reprendre sans tout relancer. En pratique, la télécommande devient presque optionnelle.

Pour le mode galerie, la bibliothèque d'œuvres d'art est payante, mais il est possible d'utiliser ses propres photos gratuitement et de les faire défiler. En zoomant avec la caméra du téléphone sur une œuvre affichée, on voit les coups de pinceau et les détails comme si c'était une vraie toile. C'est carrément bluffant. Le mode art est aussi optionnel : si on ne veut pas que la TV se transforme en cadre à la fermeture, il suffit de maintenir le bouton d'alimentation 3 secondes et la TV s'éteint complètement. Une fois que j'ai installé et configuré ma TV, j'ai envoyé une photo d'un oeuvre d'art à mon père, et il a cru pendant un court moment que c'était un très grand cadre photo. L'écran fait moins d'un pouce d'épaisseur, ce qui lui donne exactement l'apparence d'un tableau accroché au mur. Il faut se dire que moi, j'ai le contour de la TV qui est noir, mais cette TV a aussi l'option de contour en bois, ce qui rendrait sa encore plus difficile à savoir qu'il s'agît en réalité d'un TV et si on ajoute à sa qu'on passe le câble dans le mur, on vient de créer un nouveau jeu similaire au jeux "AI or not" : TV ou Cadre.

Je n'ai qu'un seul câble de branché pour que tout fonctionne, pas besoin d'un câble pour l'alimentation de la TV, d'un câble pour la barre de son etc, donc c'est très minimaliste.

Note : Le son et la qualité d'image dans la vidéo a mal été filmé par mon cellulaire car il n'est pas très récent, je vous assure que l'image ne n'est pas saturé comme ça (les photos prisent en sont la preuve) et que l'audio est 1000 fois meilleure que dans ma vidéo.

title: An Advanced Display Designed as Much for the Room as for the Viewer
body:
The Samsung Frame Pro is an advanced display designed as much for the room as for the viewer. Rather than simply producing another premium television, Samsung has clearly focused on creating a display that integrates into your living space without giving up the performance expected from a modern high-end TV.

Packaging was excellent, with everything needed for installation including the flush wall mount, tabletop feet, wireless hub, remote and accessories. The television itself is exceptionally thin and surprisingly heavy for its size, so I would strongly recommend two people for installation and lifting only by the frame edges.

The wireless hub is one of the standout features. HDMI devices, Ethernet, optical audio, antenna and USB storage all connect to the hub rather than directly to the television, allowing the display itself to remain almost cable-free with only a single visible power cable. It makes for an exceptionally clean installation and means adding or changing devices happens at the cabinet instead of behind a flush-mounted TV.

Initial setup took a little patience. Like many modern smart devices, the TV immediately performed a substantial firmware update. I encountered a few networking quirks during the very first setup (before updating), but once updated everything operated normally. This feels like the sort of one-time setup experience that many connected devices go through today rather than an ongoing issue.

The defining feature for me is the display itself. The anti-glare surface is unlike any television I’ve personally used. Instead of creating sharp, mirror-like reflections, overhead lights become soft, diffuse illumination that quickly disappears into the image once content is playing. Even more impressive is that Samsung accomplished this without noticeably softening the picture. Small text remained crisp, colours stayed accurate, and I found myself comfortably reading code and working from well off-center under bright room lighting.

Art Mode is what finally made the purpose of the Frame Pro click for me. Years ago, modern televisions reached the point where people walked into a showroom and said “wow” because of how impressive they looked while turned on. The Frame Pro gave me that same reaction while it was effectively “off.” Rather than looking like a large black rectangle hanging on the wall, it genuinely becomes part of the room. Samsung promotes its Art Store subscription, but you’re not locked into it, you can also load your own artwork or photos from USB storage.

Movie performance was equally impressive. I tested everything from high-contrast films like Sin City to modern, visually demanding movies with fast action and expansive scenery. The AI picture processing adapted well to different content, motion remained smooth, colours were rich without looking exaggerated, and the display was equally comfortable to watch in a bright daytime living room or a dark evening movie session.

Gaming exceeded my expectations as well. Connected to a PC, the display automatically negotiated 4K at 144 Hz, with higher refresh rates available at lower resolutions (although I did not specifically test 240 Hz operation). Detail, colour, responsiveness and smooth camera movement were all excellent, and the wireless hub introduced no noticeable lag or display issues while changing resolutions or switching between systems. The forgiving viewing angles and excellent anti-glare characteristics also make it a very comfortable display for casual couch gaming.

One use case that mattered to me was how naturally this television lends itself to becoming an “ephemeral workstation.” Pair the hub with a compact mini-PC or NUC tucked away in a cabinet, add a wireless keyboard and mouse or trackball, and the television becomes a clean, cable-free workstation when needed, then quietly returns to displaying artwork when you’re finished. The same concept works equally well for game streaming or a compact entertainment PC.

Sound quality is very nice for a TV alone, and would be perfectly fine without needing to be paired with a sound bar or external system, although they would offer enhanced sound experience.

This isn’t the television for someone who simply wants the biggest, brightest display that dominates the room. Samsung makes other models that lean more heavily in that direction. The Frame Pro takes a different approach. It impresses with subtlety. It delivers excellent performance for movies, television, gaming and even light workstation use while integrating into your living space in a way that no conventional television I’ve used has managed.

After spending time with it, I came away more impressed than I expected. It’s a premium display that successfully bridges high-performance entertainment with thoughtful interior design, and it accomplishes that goal remarkably well.

author: Kelly M

title: Impressive Art TV
body:
I was looking for a TV that would fit the aesthetic of my dining room, and this one is honestly beautiful. The installation process was straightforward using the included wall mount. Samsung includes a positioning guide in the box, which helped me align everything properly on the wall. One of the features I appreciate the most is the One Connect Box. Since it is separate from the TV, the only cable running to the screen is the power cable, which helps keep the setup looking very clean. I was able to place the One Connect Box inside a cabinet, making the installation even more discreet. After mounting the TV, I went through the setup process. It prompted me to use the SmartThings app on my phone, but unfortunately the setup failed twice. I ended up completing everything directly on the TV instead, and that worked without any issues.

Once the setup was finished, I pressed the power button on the remote and was immediately blown away by the Art Mode. I still cannot get over how realistic it looks. Unless I tell people it is a TV, most assume it is simply a large framed artwork hanging on the wall. That is really what makes this TV special. Art Mode automatically activates when you turn the TV off, and it works very well. There is an extensive built-in art gallery available through a subscription service, but you can also upload your own artwork and photos through the SmartThings app or by using a USB drive connected to the One Connect Box.

As for picture quality, it is excellent. The 4K image is incredibly sharp, and the QLED Mini LED panel with HDR delivers vibrant colors, impressive brightness, and excellent contrast. What is even more impressive is how matte the screen looks in Art Mode while still providing such a great picture quality when watching content. For gamers, the TV also supports up to 144Hz, although I did not test that feature since mine is installed in the dining room. Another nice feature is the anti-glare coating. Even with direct sunlight coming into the room, the screen remains easy to view. Watching darker movies during the day is not an issue at all.

The only aspect I do not particularly like is the software experience. The interface feels somewhat cluttered with features and recommendations I never use. Samsung TV Plus comes pre-installed and cannot be removed or hidden. There are also a lot of ads for renting or buying movie or shows that cannot be removed. The overall UI also feel a little bit slow and sluggish comparing to an Apple TV for example. That said, it can be worked around since you can simply connect a streaming device of your choice to the One Connect Box and bypass most of the built-in software experience. Doing so does not affect Art Mode in any way.

Overall, I think this is an excellent TV for anyone who wants the benefits of a modern television without compromising the look and aesthetic of their room.

body:

The home menu offers a lot of customization options. I was able to add my streaming services easily, and I was happy to see AI integrations available, including Copilot and Perplexity. One of my favorite features so far is Art Mode. The included artwork options look great, and I like that there are additional collections available if you want more variety.

The only frustrating part was the initial setup. If you don’t already have a Samsung account, you’ll need to create one to access all of the features. I had an old account that I needed to recover, and it took several attempts and about 15 minutes before everything was finally connected and working properly.

Once setup was complete, the experience was seamless. The TV connected to both my Samsung account and my son’s account, and I like that we can use our phones as remotes in addition to the included remote control.

We intend to mount this in our kitchen/dining area, and I think the Art Mode feature will work especially well there. I’m looking forward to displaying artwork when the TV isn’t in use and using it to stream music with a nice background image in the evenings.

Since we’ve only recently set it up, I haven’t used it long enough to comment on long-term performance or reliability. However, my initial impressions are very positive, and I’ll update my review if my experience changes over time.

title: Amazing picture quality. I hate the OS
body:
TL;DR

Amazing picture quality with different picture modes for different types of content and lighting conditions. Impressive sound quality for a TV. Annoying OS and Home Screen.

In depth review and initial thoughts:

This tv is a HUGE improvement over my previous one- which was a Samsung UN55C5000 from 2010.. that being said my old tv was still in great shape and still had an acceptable image quality- so even though this new tv is definitely on the pricey side I have confidence that it should last me quite some time.

Even though I have been daily driving a 16 year old tv, over the years I have seen my fair share of televisions. 4k smart TVs are kind of a dime a dozen these days- you can buy them for a couple hundred dollars at pretty much any retailer - but that doesn’t mean they are all created equal. Many have left me less than impressed with the image quality, and the “smart features” were usually clunky. I didn’t want to spend a couple hundred dollars for a small “upgrade” that would probably need to be replaced in a couple years. I wanted something that made me fall in love with tv and watching films again.

And that’s where this Samsung 65” QN80H comes in.

From the first time turning it on I was captivated by then colours, brightness and clarity. I will admit, I do hate how you need to set up and make accounts for everything these days. It’s super annoying, it takes like half an hour to get everything sorted: making a new Samsung account only to find out I already have an account for some super old phone or device from who knows when. I of course can’t remember the password, so I’m making a new account or doing the password recovery thing… tedious. Luckily, the Tv is super responsive to input commands from the menu. Everything feels very snappy. I’ve used cheaper TVs and trying to navigate anything is super slow and sluggish- that is absolutely not the case here, so that took some of the pain away from the set up.

Then of course I need to sign into all my streaming accounts- which isn’t too bad, and just something you need to do with new devices regardless so no point complaining there. Again, the responsiveness made it not as bad. What was bad though was just trying to navigate the OS in general and the App Store in particular. That experience was frustrating. I had to scroll through WAY TOO MANY apps to find the ones I wanted. The search would only search for content. Then you finally find the app you want, install it and “add it to Home Screen” so it takes you back to the Home Screen, then you need to go back to the app selection and scroll through everything AGAIN. Super super annoying.

Now that I’ve got my main apps downloaded and signed in, I can actually start exploring the TV. I have a few more annoyances before I get into the good… but I promise despite all these annoyances I do really like this- it’s just unfortunate that these initial interactions are the first things I have to deal with.

The main OS screen shows you all kinds of shows- from some from streaming services you have, but mostly from ones I don’t. What’s worse is that it will show me movies or shows that ARE on a service I have (in this case Crave) but it doesn’t tell me it’s on crave, instead tells me I can rent or buy it on Amazon Prime or Apple TV. I don’t think you can change this either. Ideally your Home Screen would ONLY show you things from services you have installed/ are logged in to so that you could seamlessly just use your tv to browse all the content from across all the services you have. Instead it just makes the main page frustrating and useless, and I still need to resort to third party apps on my phone when searching for specific shows and trying to find if they’re on a service i have already. Right now the Home Screen is basically a store front/ advertisement, which I personally dislike… a lot.

While we’re still on the topic of the menu: it does have a bunch of different features at the top- live channels, music, to connect Spotify, gaming, art, and apps.

Live channels has a bunch of live stuff from the Samsung plus. It’s mostly just easy to watch mindless reality-esque stuff on “channels” that play different episodes of the same show over and over. Not for everyone, but sometimes some nice trash! I believe it also features local new channels which is actually nice.

The Spotify stuff is self explanatory: connect your Spotify account and listen to music. I definitely wouldn’t be buying this tv just to listen to music, but it’s a nice option to have built in and the sound quality is actually pretty good!

Gaming has both integrated free basic games you can play with your remote to cloud based streaming things via stuff like Xbox and GeForce, which is kind of cool. I only have played some of the free built in games like Tetris and word jumble game but it was interesting. My wife and I played one of the games for like 2 hours and lost track of time. Very cool! I probably won’t use the cloud gaming stuff as I have a pretty beefy pc I play on myself already, and I sure don’t need ANOTHER subscription or account to pay for and keep track of.

The art I guess is art work you can display on your tv when not in use. Samsung make the “frame” tv, so this makes lots of sense for that. I don’t mount my tv on my wall because I don’t like looking up at my tv when I’m watching it. I guess if you’re one of those people and don’t want a big black rectangle on the wall when the tv isn’t in use then this would be handy. Personally, I don’t care about it.

We’ve already touched on the apps. One more thing to mention is there’s just SO MANY… scrolling at full speed (which is fast) takes over 10 seconds to get through the whole list. The fact that I can’t easily search that list is nuts.

Now that we’ve explored the TV, let’s talk about the picture quality: it’s fantastic. It’s so bright, and the colours are so vibrant. The blacks are pretty black (not quite OLED levels, but definitely nothing you’ll really notice without pixel peeping). It has a handful of different picture modes that you can change between depending on the content and when/ where you’re viewing it. Some stuff I like to watch on dynamic, other I used the Filmmaker mode. I found during the day with bright windows I liked the dynamic setting even for movies, while at night the same movie was too bright and punchy but looked amazing on filmmaker mode- while during the day the filmmaker mode was too dim.

The picture is super crisp and sharp. The viewing angle is best from head on- but it’s definitely more than acceptably viewable at any angle you’d reasonably be watching this from. I don’t game on this- but if I did, the higher refresh rate would be an appreciated feature for devices that allowed it.

The auto adjustment features are actually kind of nice, to adjust different lighting conditions and time of day so you’re not having to constantly be doing it yourself.

The audio quality as I already touched on is great for a tv. It sounds full yet everything can be clearly heard. I’m not an audiophile and a little hard of hearing so I can’t really comment on the nuances - but it carry’s through a room pretty well, and provides more than acceptable quality out of the box for regular viewing, though I’m sure lots of people will opt for external audio speakers and solutions for that real cinematic experience.

I personally hate the clear motion, or whatever the motion smoothing is called on this TV. I hate it on all TVs and turn it off immediately. It might be good for sports- I don’t really watch sports though so I’m not sure. While we’re on the subject of turning things off— do yourself a favour a poke around the privacy controls. There’s some settings you will definitely want to disable. Google them for the latest names and what they essentially do- but the big one (which is on most smart TVs) is the one that essentially takes screenshots of your screen every few seconds and breaks it down for ai to analyze it so that you can get oddly specific ads based on everything you do on your tv, whether is via streaming or not. Big brother is watching. Disable that. Every smart device or anything connected to the internet is basically spying on you. It probably still will be in some way, but learn about and be aware of what your devices are tracking.

Overall, I am very happy with this tv, despite most my review being complaining about things. A lot of people seem to be frustrated with the OS stuff as well and get a third party solution like an Apple TV or Firestick, which I understand but also think it kind of defeats the purpose of a smart TV. I don’t know how it compares to most other smart TV OS’s, but because of the OS I am removing one star. I wish I could remove 1.25 or so, since I think this issue is worth more than a 1 star reduction but not worth 2. Without these OS issues this would easily be a 5 star TV worth the money.

title: Very Impressive Quality, but Also a Quite Expensive Mini LED TV
body:
The Samsung QN80H is a very impressive Mini LED TV thanks to its high brightness, and premium looking picture quality. The Quantum Mini LED panel gives the image a very clean and refined look, especially with higher quality content like 4K HDR10+ movies, and games. During darker settings, like the evening or when you can limit the natural light in the room, the picture can get surprisingly close to OLED quality, with good contrast and depth. I found the Filmmaker Mode to be the best-looking and most detailed picture option when the room is not too bright, but during the day I sometimes have to switch to Standard or other brighter modes because it can look a bit dim when there's too much natural light (especially when watching content with darker scenes). I would avoid using the AI Auto modes for picture, as they tend to make the picture look washed out and worsens the overall quality of the content you're watching.

Compared to some of last year's OLEDs, like the Samsung S90F and LG C5 OLED TVs, the QN80H holds up better than I expected, but the OLEDs still have the edge overall. The QN80H gets very bright, handles daytime viewing well, and does not have the same long-term burn-in concerns that some people still worry about with OLEDs. This makes it a better option for brighter rooms, but you will still need to adjust the picture during the day if you have large windows that bring in a natural light. However, OLEDs still have better black levels, more precise contrast, and that extra depth since each pixel can turn off individually (which can't for this TV). Since the QN80H is under $1800 and the both of last year's OLED models are just barely more at closer to $2000, it's hard to justify the QN80H unless you are really worried about the potential burn-in with OLEDs often watch TV in bright environments, or find this TV on a better sale.

Compared to Samsung's lower end Mini LEDs, like the M80H and M70H, the QN80H is a better performing Mini LED option. The picture looks more refined than both the M70H and M80H, with better contrast, better overall depth, and a more premium look thanks to the Quantum Mini LED panel. That said, the M80H does get surprisingly close for nearly half the price, which this TV a worse value value than the M80H for most people. The M70H on the other hand is a much more budget version, with a worse picture, only a 60Hz panel, and a less premium experience overall. The QN80H is the better TV, but the M80H makes the price jump harder to justify.

Setup was mostly straightforward, but Samsung’s account and SmartThings process can slow things down if you don't already have an account. If you have a Samsung account ready and a Samsung device connected to the WiFi, setup can be around 5-10 minutes, but creating a new Samsung account without any connected devices seemed to make it take closer to 15-20 minutes. The built-in sound is pretty good for a flat-panel TV, but with a TV this nice I would still recommend at least external speakers, and ideally an AVR with larger speakers. I also like Samsung’s Tizen software overall, but wish it supported downloading popular VPN apps like you can on Google TV. That said, if you want to use a VPN you'll need to use one of the supported or look into using an external Google TV streaming box.

Overall, the QN80H is a really good TV with a great picture quality, strong brightness, fast performance, and great gaming support. It is also one of the best-performing Mini LED options from Samsung's 2026 line-up, but just make sure you appreciate the improvement over the M80H and want to take the jump to OLED.

Pros:

- Great picture quality with strong brightness, vibrant colours and sharp details.

- Quantum Mini LED gives the image a more premium look and gets surprisingly close to OLED quality in controlled lighting.

- 144Hz support, with a powerful processor is great for gaming.

- Built-in sound is pretty good for most average viewing.

- Great all-around TV for movies, sports, gaming, and streaming.

Cons:

- At under $1800, it is very close to OLED pricing without OLED performance, and quite a bit more than the more affordable M80H.

- AI display modes seem to make the picture look washed out.

- Filmmaker Mode looks great in controlled lighting, but can look dim with darker content during the day.

- Samsung account/SmartThings creation can really slow down the setup if not created ahead of time.

- Most popular VPN apps require an external Google TV box.

title: sharp image, brilliant colours
body:
We ordered the QN900F 65in Samsung TV to replace an older, somewhat smaller 55in that decided to move out with our son. The screen is noticeably larger, huge. My wife thought it may have been too large for our smallish living room but I think she’s getting used to it after being glued to it this past weekend watching a couple of her beloved cricket games.

The Samsung name provides a certain sense of quality. The unit is solidly put together with a clean and simple-looking design. There are ample connections on the back including 4 HDMI ports, two USB ports, a network port and a digital audio port. The tiny remote can be programmed to turn your cable box on and off with the TV which is convenient but it lacks the numbered keypad your cable box remote probably has for letting you quickly punch in channel numbers. It does, however, provide up/down toggles for changing volume and channels. Those same buttons also control a couple of other functions like Mute which is a nice feature. A selector dial on the remote lets you scroll through menus when needed. The remote also sports several dedicated buttons for services such as YouTube and Netflix. The remote is rechargeable via a USB cable, surprisingly NOT included with the TV, or through turning it over and letting it charge via the small solar panel on its back. I’m honestly not sure if that qualifies as an amazing innovation or mere gimmick but it’s there.

Setup and connection was relatively easy. I mounted the TV on our living room TV stand and plugged in our cable box, the hard drive I keep a few digital movies on, a DVD player and so on. Everything seems to work as expected. Finding my movie drive involved a bit of a search and drilling down to find, well, any movie seemed like a somewhat more cumbersome process than it should have been but the TV had no problem playing them and I suppose after watching a couple of movies, we’ll get used to Samsung’s process. The bluetooth feature is another very convenient and useful one. With that retired 55inch, we had to use a USB stick plugged into a digital audio converter to enable my wife’s wireless bluetooth headset to work. With this Samsung TV, the headset connects directly to the TV when she wants to watch something without disturbing anyone else in the house.

Out of the box, however, the picture quality was sadly not that impressive. I’m not sure why Samsung set the default to what must be their lowest settings but the picture was grainy and the colours somehow washed out yet too bright at the same time. A romp though the settings tab led me to the picture mode options, however, and I was immediately much happier after changing the mode. Finer adjustments may be possible but I haven’t dug in that deeply yet. Watching now, the colours are vibrant and brilliantly sharp with deep velvety blacks and wonderful contrast. Even in our sunny living room, it pops. We tend to watch a lot of nature documentaries and while they are typically broadcast only in HD, they still look amazing on this 8K beast. As I don’t have any 4K disks I can’t comment on that or the native resolution. Sound quality is very good, we think, and easily fills the room if we need it to while remaining crisp and clear. Audiophiles or folks building a home theatre may want a surround-sound setup but the TV’s built-in speakers sound just perfectly good to us.

I do have a couple of negatives I would mention: The printed documentation in the box was disappointing. The manual, for example, says precious little about actually operating the TV or navigating it’s menus. Guides are available from the Home screen on the TV, however, which teach you about features and usage of the TV and remote. That’s convenient, but I still like paper manuals for the simple old school ability to make a note. More disappointing are the frankly invasive permissions Samsung demands simply to use the product as a TV. Users must agree to allow Samsung to collect as much data about you and your usage of the TV as they wish in order to allow them and their partners to better target you with ads in all of their related cross-platform apps and services. I don’t want that, but there was no obvious option to refuse other than to simply not use the TV. Irritating for me but I know many people won’t be too bothered.

My concerns aside, we are eminently pleased with how good this TV performs with its giant screen, bright and brilliant colours, and clear sound.

Lastly, the TV comes with 2 L-shaped feet/legs that slide into the back of the TV's frame. There are 4 positions so they can be close together or far wide apart predicated on table space, that's if you don't plan on having this wall mounted. I do plan on wall mounting this, so there's 4 standard VESA mount screw holes on the back.

The TV itself is pretty heavy at just under 57 lbs.

title: A Glimpse into the Future of Television, Today.
body:
I've never been impressed by a TV, but this TV got me in total awe. My goal was to build a home theater centerpiece that was as future-proof as possible, and I can say without hesitation, this TV has exceeded every expectation. It's less of a television and more of a visual experience.

The 8K resolution of this TV is simply stunning. While native 8K content is still scarce, the AI Gen 3 Processor did a phenomenal job in upscaling non 8K contents. It takes high-quality 4K contents and gives them a level of sharpness and depth I've never seen before. It delivers incredible color and contrast.

The Mini LED technology delivers, the blacks are inky deep black, and the bright pop without any blooming or halo effects. The Glare Free screen is another huge win; my living room gets a lot of natural light, and it handles the reflections with no issue.

The TV itself, with its razor-thin "Infinity Design" bezel, looks like a floating sheet of glass.

Gaming on a Nintendo or other console is a dream. The 240Hz refresh rate makes everything incredibly fluid and responsive. There's no motion blur, just crisp, smooth action. I paired the TV with a soundbar, and the Q-Symphony feature, which uses both the TV speakers and the soundbar in harmony, creates a rich, immersive soundstage that genuinely fills the room.

Perhaps the most underrated feature is the Wireless One Connect box. It's revolutionary. It allow all my devices (Nintendo Switch, Google TV, DVD player) plug into this separate unit, which communicates with the TV wirelessly. This allowed me to mount the TV on the wall with absolutely no visible cable clutter or a mess of cables running down. It creates an incredibly clean and minimalist look that you can't achieve with other televisions.

I also like the AI built into this TV, like 'click to search', which allows me to find content easier. 'Live translate' also is another AI improvement which translate language to another, when the content is playing in another language than English.

I also love that SmartThings is supported on this TV, where the TV acts as a hub where I can control my smart home devices.

The TV can also display art content to make it like an Art Frame which is super cool.

The only real "con" is the price tag—this is undeniably a premium, flagship product, and the cost reflects that. And while the upscaling is magical, we're all still waiting for the world to catch up with more native 8K content. However, this TV is a major way to future proof one's purchase.
